Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations

Hajime Seya Address: Kobe University, Kobe, Japan    Ryosei Moriwaki Address: Kobe University, Kobe, Japan    Daisuke Murakami Address: The Institute of Statistical Mathematics, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract

Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. Without a pre-treatment trajectory to match, choosing donor weights for such post-only locations requires an additional source of information. We propose Graph-SCM, which estimates donor weights jointly across treated locations and encourages geographically neighboring locations to use similar donor combinations. GeoEco-SCM keeps the same geographic graph but adjusts the strength of its existing edges using pre-treatment economic similarity. Both methods handle complete, partial, and absent histories within one convex weight-estimation problem. Monte Carlo experiments compare them with covariate-balanced synthetic controls, equally weighted donor averages, ordinary synthetic control where estimable, and nonseparable spatio-temporal imputation and direct prediction. No method dominates. Graph-based borrowing improves on covariate balancing in several settings, but a selective-coverage design favors covariate balancing. Economic adjustment helps when geography alone misses relevant donor relationships. The results support graph regularization as a way to extend synthetic-control coverage when connected locations share similar donor representations, with its usefulness depending on the structure of the available information.

Keywords: 
spatial causal inference , synthetic control , missing pre-treatment outcomes , graph Laplacian , harmonic extension , spatio-temporal kriging

1 Introduction

Synthetic control methods (SCM) estimate an untreated counterfactual by choosing a convex combination of untreated donor units whose pre-treatment outcomes resemble those of a treated unit [1, 2]. The pre-treatment trajectory is therefore not merely a descriptive input: it is the main source of information used to determine the donor representation, meaning the target’s vector of donor weights. This creates a difficult but common problem in spatial panels. A treated location may enter an outcome database only after an intervention. Examples include newly sampled land-price points, newly observed monitoring locations, or spatial records whose historical geocoding is incomplete. Such a location can be observed in the post-treatment period while having no own pre-treatment outcome trajectory. We refer to this observation pattern as post-only. We use PRE and POST to denote the pre-treatment and post-treatment periods, respectively.

The post-only case is qualitatively different from ordinary intermittent missingness. If target ii has no observed outcome in any pre-treatment period, the usual criterion for matching pre-treatment outcomes contains no target-specific fitting information. Consequently, the donor weights are not uniquely determined: every feasible weight vector satisfies the same target-specific criterion. Here we focus on weights learned from pre-treatment outcomes; observed covariates can provide a separate balancing criterion. Dropping such locations avoids the need to construct their counterfactuals, but changes the population covered by the analysis. This becomes particularly important when historical data availability is associated with spatial or economic characteristics. In such settings, excluding post-only locations changes the target population and, when treatment effects are heterogeneous, may also change the average treatment effect being estimated.

The key idea is to borrow information about donor weights across locations. Because the graph links targets, local PRE information can guide combinations of geographically distant, unaffected donors. Nearby treated locations with observed pre-treatment histories can provide information about which donor combinations are plausible if donor relationships vary smoothly over space.

We exploit this idea through graph-regularized synthetic control (Graph-SCM). Treated locations are connected by a geographic graph, and the donor weights for all locations are estimated jointly. The usual pre-treatment matching criterion determines the weights at locations with observed histories, while a graph penalty discourages large differences in donor weights between geographically connected locations. Consequently, a post-only location can borrow information from connected locations with observed pre-treatment outcomes rather than being dropped from the analysis or having its missing outcomes imputed first.

Geographic proximity alone, however, need not imply that two locations have similar donor relationships. We therefore also propose GeoEco-SCM, an economically reweighted extension of Graph-SCM. GeoEco-SCM retains the same geographic graph but adjusts the strength of its existing connections using economic characteristics measured before treatment. Connections between geographically neighboring locations that are also economically similar receive greater relative weight, whereas connections between economically dissimilar neighbors are weakened. Thus, economic information changes how strongly donor weights are shared across geographically connected locations without changing which locations are connected.

Complete, partial, and absent PRE histories are handled within the same convex estimation problem: each location contributes the outcome-matching terms available for it, and the graph links the donor representations across locations. Economic covariates then adjust this sharing locally along existing edges. This provides a common constrained formulation for heterogeneous historical coverage.

This construction has three useful features for spatial statistics. First, local similarity is represented by a graph Laplacian, a standard way to impose smoothness on irregular spatial supports [8]. Second, if a location has no pre-treatment outcomes, the graph penalty makes its donor weights a weighted combination of donor weights propagated from connected locations with observed histories. In graph terminology this weighted-average interpolation is a discrete harmonic extension [29], but its substantive meaning is simply that observed-history locations provide the information that is passed through the graph. For graph-based borrowing to reach a post-only location, that location must be connected, directly or indirectly, to a location with observed pre-treatment outcomes. Third, the graph penalty is imposed on the donor weights across locations. It therefore makes a different modeling assumption from spatial kriging or spatial matrix completion. Section 4 gives the precise interpolation conditions and the corresponding equations.

The paper makes four contributions. First, we formulate the post-only SCM problem and propose a joint graph-regularized estimator for all treated locations. Second, we explain how information reaches a post-only location through the graph and state the connectivity condition needed for this interpolation to be well defined. Third, we extend the method so that pre-treatment economic similarity can weaken or strengthen existing geographic connections without changing the graph topology. Fourth, we use a structured Monte Carlo study to identify when graph-based borrowing helps and when it does not. Five primary data-generating processes (DGPs) examine geographic smoothness, economic information, selective observation, complex donor dynamics, and a failure of spatial smoothness. Five additional stress tests are retained in the Online Appendix.

2 Relation to existing approaches

2.1 Synthetic control with incomplete pre-treatment information

Many standard SCM formulations and extensions use treated-unit pre-treatment information to learn donor relationships. Augmented SCM combines SCM balancing with an outcome-model correction [9]; partially pooled and staggered-adoption formulations borrow across treated units but retain target-specific pre-treatment outcomes [10]; generalized synthetic control imposes an interactive fixed-effect structure on the panel [27]; and synthetic difference-in-differences combines unit and time reweighting [5]. Other refinements change how the available pre-treatment trajectory is used. For example, Sun et al. [23] study temporal aggregation of pre-treatment outcomes and propose balancing both aggregated and disaggregated series to trade off noise reduction against loss of signal. These approaches address important limitations of ordinary SCM, but their usual implementations based on pre-treatment outcomes use target PRE information and do not, without an additional cross-location or covariate restriction, determine a site-specific donor representation for a target with no own PRE observations.

In empirical spatial applications, another practical response is to restrict the analysis to locations observed throughout the study period. For example, Kanasugi and Ushijima [17], in studying the effect of a high-speed railway on residential land prices, construct a balanced panel for 2008–2015 and explicitly exclude land-price points that newly enter or disappear during the analysis period. This avoids the need to construct counterfactuals for locations without a usable pre-treatment history, but it also changes the population represented by the analysis. The post-only problem considered here instead asks whether such locations can be retained and assigned a counterfactual under an explicit cross-location restriction.

A closely related line of work studies missing pre-treatment outcomes directly. Robust SCM first denoises and completes a noisy panel by singular-value thresholding [4]. Liu et al. [19] study conventional SCM when pre-treatment outcomes are missing. Using the vertical-regression representation of SCM, they characterize the bias that can arise when units with incomplete pre-treatment data are excluded and develop a sensitivity-analysis framework for assessing the robustness of the resulting treatment-effect estimates. This is particularly relevant to empirical practice because it formalizes the consequences of restricting the analysis to units with usable pre-treatment histories. Their objective, however, is to assess sensitivity to missing pre-treatment data and the associated sample exclusion, rather than to construct donor weights for a treated target that has no own pre-treatment trajectory. The post-only pattern considered here has no observed PRE outcome for the target, so the target-specific SCM fit term disappears and an additional source of cross-location information is needed to determine the target’s donor representation.

The closest causal-identification result to a genuinely post-only target is the proximal synthetic-control approach of Liu et al. [18]. Under proxy and bridge conditions, their framework can identify causal effects using post-intervention surrogates, even in settings with no treated-unit pre-intervention outcomes. The identifying information is fundamentally different from ours. Proximal SCM borrows through post-treatment proxy restrictions. Our estimator does not use the post-treatment outcome of a post-only target to learn its weights; instead, it borrows the donor representation from other treated locations through a graph constructed from geography and pre-treatment or treatment-invariant covariates.

2.2 Matrix completion and spatial missing-data methods

Matrix-completion approaches regard unobserved counterfactuals as missing entries of a structured panel. Nuclear-norm methods impose low rank [6]; latent-factor methods allow general missing patterns and provide inferential tools [26]; and causal matrix completion studies non-random observation mechanisms [3]. These methods borrow through a common low-dimensional outcome surface.

Spatial matrix completion adds another relevant perspective. Vu et al. [25] develop a matrix-completion method for spatially misaligned, high-dimensional air-pollution data, combining low-rank structure with spatial dependence to fill missing pollutant measurements. While their study is developed for spatially misaligned and incomplete pollution data rather than for synthetic-control estimation, it provides an important example of how spatial structure and missing observations can be incorporated jointly within a unified estimation framework. A closer precursor in the synthetic-control literature is the SMaC approach of Grossi et al. [13], which imputes treated-area counterfactual time series as weighted averages of control time series while allowing the weights to vary smoothly over space through a Gaussian-process structure.

Graph-SCM places the structural restriction at a different level. It keeps the usual SCM representation

Yi​t​(0)≈𝒘i⊤​𝒀tC,Y_{it}(0)\approx\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}, (1)

where Yi​t​(0)Y_{it}(0) denotes the untreated potential outcome for target location ii at time tt, 𝒀tC\bm{Y}_{t}^{C} denotes the vector of observed outcomes for the untreated donor units at time tt, and 𝒘i\bm{w}_{i} is the corresponding vector of donor weights for target location ii. As in conventional SCM, the elements of 𝒘i\bm{w}_{i} are nonnegative and sum to one. Collecting the target-specific weight vectors as rows gives the target-by-donor weight matrix 𝑾\bm{W}. Graph-SCM regularizes this matrix across locations by encouraging geographically connected targets to have similar donor-weight patterns. In simple terms, matrix-completion methods impose structure on the outcome matrix to recover missing entries, whereas Graph-SCM imposes spatial structure on the donor weights used to construct the untreated potential outcomes in Eq. (1). These modeling structures can both be appropriate for the same data-generating process, and neither method class is uniformly more general than the other.

2.3 Spatially structured donor relationships

The closest methodological precedent to Graph-SCM is the spatial vertical regression (SVR) approach of Grossi et al. [14]. SVR writes the untreated potential outcome of each treated location as a unit-specific linear regression on the control outcomes and places Gaussian-process priors on the coefficient vector associated with each control unit across treated locations. Nearby treated locations are therefore encouraged to have similar relationships with the controls, and the model can also allow spatial dependence in the residuals. This shares the central idea of Graph-SCM that donor or control relationships can themselves vary smoothly across spatially related treated locations, rather than requiring only the outcomes to be spatially smooth.

Our focus is the post-only setting. We connect treated locations through a graph and constrain their donor weights to be nonnegative and sum to one. The resulting convex weight-estimation problem makes the information passed to a post-only location explicit.

A related Bayesian extension by Grossi et al. [15] incorporates spatial information in a different way: its prior penalizes the selection of more distant control units and is embedded in a semiparametric framework intended to account for unobserved spatial confounding. This makes geographic distance informative about which donors should be selected, whereas Graph-SCM uses spatial relationships among treated targets to regularize how their donor-weight vectors vary across locations. Together with the earlier SMaC formulation of Grossi et al. [13], these contributions show that spatial information can enter synthetic-control analysis through several distinct channels: the outcome model, donor selection, or cross-target similarity in donor relationships.

A distinct recent proposal is Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control (Graph-SC) by Zhang et al. [28]. Its graph is defined over donors and regularizes coefficients assigned to similar donor trajectories, with the aim of stabilizing counterfactual representations under donor redundancy. The graph in the present paper instead lies on the target axis: it couples the weight vectors of different treated locations and supplies an interpolation rule for targets without their own outcome histories.

2.4 Spatial dependence and spillovers in synthetic control

Spatial structure has also been incorporated into SCM to address interference between units. Cao and Dowd [11] develop estimation and inference for direct treatment effects and spillover effects under a specified spillover structure. Sakaguchi and Tagawa [20] extend SCM with a spatial autoregressive panel model so that treatment can affect not only the treated unit but also other units through a spatial dependence structure; they develop Bayesian inference with regularization for both treatment and spillover effects. In that framework, the spatial-weight matrix represents propagation of outcomes and treatment spillovers across units. This use of spatial structure is different from ours: Graph-SCM currently assumes that donor outcomes are not contaminated by treatment and instead uses a graph to regularize similarities in the donor-weight vectors across treated target locations. These approaches are complementary: spillover-aware SCM addresses interference, whereas Graph-SCM addresses counterfactual construction when a target has little or no own pre-treatment outcome information.

2.5 Outcome-side spatial prediction

A closely related recent contribution is Hiramoto and Murakami [16], who combine synthetic control with block kriging for point-referenced data. Their work provides a distinct way of incorporating explicit geostatistical structure into SCM. Our focus is different: we ask how donor representations can be constructed for target locations that have no own pre-treatment outcomes.

A different strategy for the post-only problem is to treat the missing history itself as a spatial prediction problem. More generally, Vega and Nethery [24] show how Gaussian-process models can be used for causal inference with spatio-temporal panel data and relate the resulting posterior predictions to weighted combinations of observed outcomes, with weights reflecting spatial and temporal similarity. This is conceptually close to synthetic control but places the primary structure on the outcome process rather than on a target-by-donor weight field. A spatio-temporal model can likewise first predict the missing pre-treatment outcomes and then ordinary SCM can be applied to the completed history. Alternatively, the same spatio-temporal model can predict the untreated post-treatment outcome directly. We use a nonseparable covariance model from the Gneiting class [12] for both strategies. The economic-covariate benchmarks use the same types of PRE economic variables as GeoEco-SCM, but include them in the outcome mean model rather than in target-graph edge weights. The comparison therefore asks a substantive modeling question: is it more useful to model the outcome surface directly, or to borrow the donor representation across nearby locations?

3.1 Potential outcomes, donors, and observation regimes

3.2 Why ordinary SCM is underdetermined for a post-only target

For a target with at least one observed pre-treatment outcome, a simple SCM formulation based on observed pre-treatment outcomes solves

𝒘^iSCM∈arg​min𝒘∈ΔJ⁡1|𝒪i|​∑t∈𝒪i(Yi​t−𝒘⊤​𝒀tC)2.\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i}^{\mathrm{SCM}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{w}\in\Delta_{J}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}}\left(Y_{it}-\bm{w}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}\right)^{2}. (10)

If 𝒪i=∅\mathcal{O}_{i}=\varnothing, define the empty-history extension of this fitting loss to be zero, without dividing by |𝒪i||\mathcal{O}_{i}|. It is then constant over the simplex, so that formally arg​min𝒘∈ΔJ⁡0=ΔJ\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{w}\in\Delta_{J}}0=\Delta_{J}. The optimization problem is therefore not undefined; rather, the target-specific representation is completely underdetermined by the target’s own PRE outcomes. This is a structural absence of the matching criterion, not a numerical convergence problem.

Discarding post-only targets changes the population over which the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) is evaluated. If Ri=1R_{i}=1 denotes having any pre-treatment outcome, then the estimand based only on analyzable targets is

A​T​TPRE​(t)=E⁡[τi​t∣Ri=1],ATT_{\mathrm{PRE}}(t)=E[\tau_{it}\mid R_{i}=1], (11)

whereas the policy estimand for all treated targets is

A​T​TALL​(t)=E⁡[τi​t].ATT_{\mathrm{ALL}}(t)=E[\tau_{it}]. (12)

These two quantities can differ when historical coverage is associated with treatment-effect heterogeneity. The target locations are assumed to be definable independently of treatment; the framework does not cover entities whose existence is caused by the intervention.

4 Graph-regularized synthetic control

The procedure has four steps. First, construct a graph between target locations from geography and, for GeoEco-SCM, PRE economic attributes. Second, use held-out PRE outcomes to select how strongly neighboring targets share donor weights and how much economic similarity modifies the geographic edges (Section 6). Third, fit all target weights together using the available PRE outcomes. Finally, combine each target’s fitted weights with donor POST outcomes to predict its untreated path. Target POST outcomes enter only afterward, when treatment effects are calculated.

4.1 Roles of assumptions and support conditions

The method combines two substantive modeling requirements with two support and design conditions. The donor representation must remain useful from PRE to POST (Assumption 1), and connected targets should have similar donor representations (Assumption 2). Graph-based borrowing also requires a path from each post-only target to an observed-history target (Condition 1), while geography and economic covariates must be available independently of target POST outcomes (Condition 2). These requirements concern donor validity, the plausibility of borrowing, and the information available to the estimator.

For partial histories, the observed PRE periods must be informative about the donor relationship of interest. As in conventional SCM, causal interpretation additionally requires no anticipation and donor outcomes that remain untreated and are not materially contaminated by treatment spillovers.

4.2 Baseline SCM representation and the additional graph restriction

The first assumption is inherited from ordinary SCM. Its purpose is to formalize two familiar requirements: the donor pool must provide a useful convex representation of each target, and that representation must remain informative from the pre-treatment period into the post-treatment period.

Assumption 1 (Baseline SCM donor support and temporal stability).

For each target location ii, there exists a donor-weight vector 𝐰i⋆∈ΔJ\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}\in\Delta_{J} such that

Yi​t​(0)=𝒘i⋆⁣⊤​𝒀tC+ξi​t,t∈𝒯0∪𝒯1,Y_{it}(0)=\bm{w}_{i}^{\star\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}+\xi_{it},\qquad t\in\mathcal{T}_{0}\cup\mathcal{T}_{1}, (13)

where Yi​t​(0)Y_{it}(0) is the untreated potential outcome of target ii at time tt, 𝐘tC\bm{Y}_{t}^{C} is the JJ-dimensional vector of donor outcomes at time tt, and ξi​t\xi_{it} is the approximation error, that is, the part of the untreated outcome not reproduced by the donor combination. The approximation is assumed to be sufficiently accurate for the counterfactual prediction problem of interest.

Because 𝒘i⋆∈ΔJ\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}\in\Delta_{J}, its elements are nonnegative and sum to one. Thus the synthetic control is a convex combination of donor outcomes rather than an unrestricted linear extrapolation across donors. At the same time, SCM still extrapolates the donor relationship learned before treatment into the post-treatment period. The substantive temporal restriction in Assumption 1 is therefore that the same donor-weight vector remains relevant before and after treatment. This requirement applies to ordinary SCM as well as to Graph-SCM.

Assumption 1 alone does not solve the post-only problem. If target ii has no pre-treatment outcomes, its own data provide no information for learning 𝒘i⋆\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}. Graph-SCM therefore adds a second restriction whose purpose is to justify borrowing donor-weight information across target locations.

Let G=(V,E,𝑨)G=(V,E,\bm{A}) denote an undirected weighted graph over the NN target locations. Here, V={1,…,N}V=\{1,\ldots,N\} is the set of target locations, EE is the set of undirected edges connecting target pairs, and 𝑨=(ai​k)∈ℝN×N\bm{A}=(a_{ik})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is the symmetric weighted adjacency matrix. The scalar ai​k=ak​i≥0a_{ik}=a_{ki}\geq 0 measures the strength of the connection between targets ii and kk; pairs that are not connected have ai​k=0a_{ik}=0.

Collect the true donor-weight vectors into

𝑾⋆=(𝒘1⋆,…,𝒘N⋆)⊤∈ℝN×J,\bm{W}^{\star}=(\bm{w}_{1}^{\star},\ldots,\bm{w}_{N}^{\star})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J}, (14)

so that the iith row of 𝑾⋆\bm{W}^{\star} is the donor representation of target ii.

Assumption 2 (Similarity of donor representations across connected locations).

For the graph used by the estimator,

Here, ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes the Euclidean norm. Hence ‖𝒘i⋆−𝒘k⋆‖22\|\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}-\bm{w}_{k}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2} measures how different the donor-weight vectors are at two connected targets, while ai​ka_{ik} gives greater importance to differences along stronger graph connections. A small value of ℰ𝑨​(𝑾⋆)\mathcal{E}_{\bm{A}}(\bm{W}^{\star}) therefore means that strongly connected targets tend to use similar donor combinations.

This is the main substantive assumption added by Graph-SCM. It concerns smoothness of the donor representation, not necessarily smoothness or stationarity of the observed outcome surface. If connected targets have unrelated donor representations, graph-based borrowing need not help and can introduce bias.

4.3 A common penalized estimator

We now translate the two ideas above into an estimator. Recall that 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} is the set of observed pre-treatment periods for target ii, ℐ+={i:|𝒪i|>0}\mathcal{I}_{+}=\{i:|\mathcal{O}_{i}|>0\} is the set of targets with at least one observed pre-treatment outcome, and N+=|ℐ+|N_{+}=|\mathcal{I}_{+}|. For 𝑾=(𝒘1,…,𝒘N)⊤∈ℝN×J\bm{W}=(\bm{w}_{1},\ldots,\bm{w}_{N})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J}, define the pre-treatment fitting loss

ℒfit​(𝑾)=1N+​∑i∈ℐ+1|𝒪i|​∑t∈𝒪i(Yi​t−𝒘i⊤​𝒀tC)2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fit}}(\bm{W})=\frac{1}{N_{+}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{+}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}}\left(Y_{it}-\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}\right)^{2}. (16)

Throughout, at least one target has observed PRE outcomes and the graph has positive total edge weight. The inner average measures pre-treatment fit for one target using only the periods in which that target is observed. The outer average gives each target equal weight, so a complete-history target does not dominate a partial-history target merely because it has more observed periods.

The second part of the estimator penalizes differences in donor weights across connected targets. Recall that 𝑨=(ai​k)\bm{A}=(a_{ik}) is the N×NN\times N symmetric weighted adjacency matrix of GG, with ai​k>0a_{ik}>0 for connected pairs and ai​k=0a_{ik}=0 otherwise. Define

ℰ𝑨​(𝑾)=1A+​∑(i,k)∈Eai​k​‖𝒘i−𝒘k‖22,A+=∑(i,k)∈Eai​k,\mathcal{E}_{\bm{A}}(\bm{W})=\frac{1}{A_{+}}\sum_{(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}\|\bm{w}_{i}-\bm{w}_{k}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad A_{+}=\sum_{(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}, (17)

where A+A_{+} is the total edge weight. This quantity is small when strongly connected targets have similar donor-weight vectors.

For compact matrix notation, let 𝑫=diag⁡(d1,…,dN)\bm{D}=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1},\ldots,d_{N}), where di=∑kai​kd_{i}=\sum_{k}a_{ik} is the total connection strength, or weighted degree, of target ii. The matrix

𝑳=𝑫−𝑨\bm{L}=\bm{D}-\bm{A} (18)

is the weighted graph Laplacian. This standard graph matrix summarizes which locations are connected and how strongly. With each undirected edge counted once,

∑(i,k)∈Eai​k​‖𝒘i−𝒘k‖22=tr⁡(𝑾⊤​𝑳​𝑾),\sum_{(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}\|\bm{w}_{i}-\bm{w}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{L}\bm{W}), (19)

where tr⁡(⋅)\operatorname{tr}(\cdot) denotes the matrix trace. Equation (19) is only a compact matrix expression of the pairwise penalty in Eq. (17); the substantive idea remains the same.

We use a common objective for both proposed estimators. Write 𝑨⁡(β)\bm{A}(\beta) for a target graph whose edge strengths reflect geographic proximity and can also account for pre-treatment economic similarity. The parameter β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls this economic adjustment: 𝑨⁡(0)\bm{A}(0) uses geography alone. For this geography-only case, Eqs. (17)–(19) are evaluated with 𝑨=𝑨⁡(0)\bm{A}=\bm{A}(0); the same definitions apply to the economically adjusted graph with 𝑨=𝑨⁡(β)\bm{A}=\bm{A}(\beta). Section 5 gives the graph construction. For a chosen β\beta, all graph quantities, including A+A_{+} and 𝑳\bm{L}, are computed from 𝑨⁡(β)\bm{A}(\beta); we suppress this dependence where it is clear from context.

The full estimator combines pre-treatment fit, graph-based similarity, and a small numerical ridge:

𝑾^​(λ,β,ε)∈arg​min𝑾:𝒘i∈ΔJ{ℒfit​(𝑾)+λ​ℰ𝑨⁡(β)​(𝑾)+εN​‖𝑾‖F2},\begin{split}\widehat{\bm{W}}(\lambda,\beta;\varepsilon)\in{}&\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{W}:\,\bm{w}_{i}\in\Delta_{J}}\\ &\left\{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fit}}(\bm{W})+\lambda\mathcal{E}_{\bm{A}(\beta)}(\bm{W})+\frac{\varepsilon}{N}\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}\right\},\end{split} (20)

where λ,β,ε≥0\lambda,\beta,\varepsilon\geq 0 and ‖𝑾‖F2=∑i=1N∑j=1Jwi​j2\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_{ij}^{2}. Graph-SCM fixes β=0\beta=0, so borrowing depends on geography alone. GeoEco-SCM uses the same objective but allows β\beta to be selected together with λ\lambda, so economic similarity can modify borrowing along the geographic edges. Economic information therefore enters through the graph weights, rather than through a separate fitting-loss term.

The parameter λ\lambda controls the strength of graph regularization. At locations with observed PRE histories, small values place more emphasis on their own fit, while larger values give greater influence to agreement across connected targets. A post-only target has no own fitting term and receives information through these connections.

Each target still has its own donor-weight vector. Graph regularization trades the flexibility of independent fits for information sharing: it can stabilize estimates from short histories, but can bias weights when connected targets have different donor relationships.

The final term is a numerical ridge. Short PRE histories or highly similar donor trajectories can leave several weight matrices with the same or nearly the same fitting and graph-penalty values. A positive ε\varepsilon makes the objective strictly convex, giving a unique mathematical minimizer while preserving the quadratic-program structure. On the simplex, the ridge favors less concentrated donor weights, toward equal allocation across donors. Conditional on the fitted weights at locations with observed PRE histories, post-only predictions then combine predictions propagated from those locations with the equally weighted average of donor outcomes. The mathematical details are given in the Online Appendix, Section 1.3.

In this study, we fix ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} throughout tuning and final estimation; only λ\lambda and, for GeoEco-SCM, β\beta are selected by validation. This value keeps the added penalty at most 10−1010^{-10} in the normalized objective for any feasible weights. The bound and its implications are given in the Online Appendix, Section 1.3. The following subsections first describe the borrowing mechanism in the special case ε=0\varepsilon=0, for which the interpolation formulas take a particularly simple form.

4.4 How donor-weight information reaches a post-only target

To make the borrowing mechanism explicit, fix a graph 𝑨⁡(β)\bm{A}(\beta) and consider λ>0\lambda>0 and ε=0\varepsilon=0 in Eq. (20). Separate the targets into two groups. Let 𝒜=ℐ+\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{I}_{+} denote targets with at least one observed pre-treatment outcome. We call them anchors because their donor weights are directly informed by observed PRE outcomes. Let 𝒰=ℐ0\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{I}_{0} denote post-only targets, which have no observed PRE outcomes.

Let 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} be the matrix obtained by stacking the donor-weight vectors of the anchor locations, and let 𝑾𝒰\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}} be the corresponding matrix for post-only locations. Thus, 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} contains weights informed directly by observed PRE outcomes, whereas 𝑾𝒰\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}} contains weights that must be inferred through graph borrowing.

Order the targets so that anchors come first and post-only locations second, and partition the graph Laplacian as

𝑳=(𝑳𝒜​𝒜𝑳𝒜​𝒰𝑳𝒰​𝒜𝑳𝒰​𝒰).\bm{L}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}&\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\\ \bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}&\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\end{pmatrix}. (21)

For example, 𝑳𝒰​𝒜\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}} summarizes graph connections from post-only locations to anchors, while 𝑳𝒰​𝒰\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}} summarizes connections among post-only locations.

For graph borrowing to determine a post-only weight vector, information from at least one anchor must be able to reach that location.

Condition 1 (Graph support for post-only targets).

Every post-only target is connected, directly or through other target locations, to at least one anchor. Equivalently, every connected component of the target graph G=(V,E,𝐀)G=(V,E,\bm{A}) that contains a post-only target also contains at least one anchor.

Here, a connected component means a group of locations that can be reached from one another through a sequence of graph edges. Condition 1 is directly checkable from the graph and observation pattern. If a group of post-only locations is isolated from all anchors, graph smoothness can make their weights similar to one another.

The next result formalizes what the graph penalty does once the anchor weights are held fixed. Here 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} can be any fixed matrix of feasible weights, including weights estimated from the observed data.

Proposition 1 (Donor-weight interpolation for post-only locations).

Fix a graph and simplex-valued anchor weights 𝐖𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. Consider λ>0\lambda>0 and ε=0\varepsilon=0. Under Condition 1, the post-only weights that minimize the graph penalty satisfy

𝑳𝒰​𝒰​𝑾𝒰+𝑳𝒰​𝒜​𝑾𝒜=0,\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}+\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}=0, (22)

and therefore

𝑾𝒰=𝑯​𝑾𝒜,𝑯=−𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜.\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{H}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}},\qquad\bm{H}=-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}. (23)

The entries of 𝐇\bm{H} are nonnegative and each row sums to one:

𝑯≥0,𝑯​𝟏|𝒜|=𝟏|𝒰|,\bm{H}\geq 0,\qquad\bm{H}\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{A}|}=\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{U}|}, (24)

where 𝟏m\bm{1}_{m} denotes an mm-dimensional vector of ones. Hence each post-only donor-weight vector is a convex combination of anchor donor-weight vectors and remains in ΔJ\Delta_{J}.

What Proposition 1 means

The proposition is easiest to read from right to left in Eq. (23). The rows of 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} are donor-weight vectors learned from targets that actually have PRE outcomes. The matrix 𝑯\bm{H} tells us how those anchor representations are combined for each post-only target. For example, if one row of 𝑯\bm{H} is (0.6,0.3,0.1)(0.6,0.3,0.1) for three anchors a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}, then the corresponding post-only donor vector is 0.6​𝒘a1+0.3​𝒘a2+0.1​𝒘a30.6\bm{w}_{a_{1}}+0.3\bm{w}_{a_{2}}+0.1\bm{w}_{a_{3}}. The graph therefore does not create new outcome information; it determines how existing PRE information is transported from anchors to post-only locations.

The same result can be written locally as

𝒘i=1di∑k:(i,k)∈Eai​k𝒘k,\bm{w}_{i}=\frac{1}{d_{i}}\sum_{k:(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}\bm{w}_{k}, (25)

so a post-only target’s donor-weight vector is the edge-weighted average of its neighbors’ donor-weight vectors. If some neighbors are themselves post-only, information can pass through them from more distant anchors. In graph terminology this is called a discrete harmonic extension [29]. A full proof of Proposition 1 is provided in the Online Appendix, Section 1.1.

With ε=0\varepsilon=0, the same identity holds for donor-based predictions at any date:

𝒀^𝒰​t​(0)=𝑯​𝑾^𝒜​𝒀tC=𝑯​𝒀^𝒜​t​(0).\widehat{\bm{Y}}_{\mathcal{U}t}(0)=\bm{H}\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{A}}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}=\bm{H}\widehat{\bm{Y}}_{\mathcal{A}t}(0). (26)

Thus, conditional on the fitted anchor weights, interpolating donor weights and interpolating the corresponding anchor predictions give exactly the same post-only prediction. The graph penalty also allows the weights at locations with observed PRE histories to adjust in response to one another. Proposition 2 below shows how this happens when the interpolation formula for the post-only weights is substituted into the objective.

4.5 What post-only locations contribute to the graph penalty

The following algebraic result shows how paths through post-only locations link the anchor weights.

Proposition 2 (Equivalent graph penalty after post-only interpolation).

Under Condition 1, for fixed simplex-valued 𝐖𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}, minimizing the graph penalty over 𝐖𝒰\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}} gives the solution in Proposition 1, and

min𝑾𝒰⁡tr⁡(𝑾⊤​𝑳​𝑾)\displaystyle\min_{\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{L}\bm{W}) =tr⁡(𝑾𝒜⊤​𝑳eff​𝑾𝒜),\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\left(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}\right),
𝑳eff\displaystyle\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}} =𝑳𝒜​𝒜−𝑳𝒜​𝒰​𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜.\displaystyle=\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}. (27)

Here, 𝐋eff\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}} is the effective graph Laplacian among the anchor locations after accounting for paths that pass through post-only locations.

What Proposition 2 means

For fixed anchor weights, Proposition 1 gives the post-only weights that minimize the graph penalty: 𝑾𝒰=𝑯​𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{H}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. Substituting this expression into the graph penalty gives the right-hand side of Eq. (27), which depends only on 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. Thus the optimization can be carried out over the anchor weights alone, and the post-only weights are subsequently obtained from the same interpolation formula. The post-only locations remain part of the model: paths through them determine 𝑳eff\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}} and therefore affect how the anchor weights are linked. They change these graph connections without adding PRE outcome observations. This substitution is a Schur-complement reduction, also called Kron reduction in network theory. A full proof is provided in the Online Appendix, Section 1.2.

For λ>0\lambda>0 and ε=0\varepsilon=0, substituting 𝑾𝒰=𝑯​𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{H}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} into Eq. (20) gives the equivalent optimization over anchor weights:

𝑾^𝒜∈arg​min𝒘i∈ΔJ,i∈𝒜{ℒfit​(𝑾𝒜)+λA+​tr⁡(𝑾𝒜⊤​𝑳eff​𝑾𝒜)}.\begin{split}\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in{}&\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{w}_{i}\in\Delta_{J},\ i\in\mathcal{A}}\\ &\left\{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fit}}(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}})+\frac{\lambda}{A_{+}}\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}})\right\}.\end{split} (28)

If each location with observed PRE outcomes were fitted separately, only the first term in Eq. (28) would be minimized. The second term links the donor weights across these locations through 𝑳eff\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}, so their weights are estimated together. The weights at post-only locations are then obtained from Eq. (23). This is how one formulation accommodates complete, partial, and absent PRE histories.

Equation (28) omits the ridge because it describes the case ε=0\varepsilon=0. In computation, we solve the full objective in Eq. (20), with ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} as specified in Section 4.3. The corresponding conditional interpolation, including the contribution from the equally weighted donor average, is derived in the Online Appendix, Section 1.3.

4.6 Counterfactuals and causal estimands

After estimating weights using pre-treatment information, the untreated post-treatment counterfactual is

Y^i​t​(0)=𝒘^i⊤​𝒀tC,t∈𝒯1.\widehat{Y}_{it}(0)=\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C},\qquad t\in\mathcal{T}_{1}. (29)

The site- and time-specific treatment effect estimate is

τ^i​t=Yi​t−Y^i​t​(0),\widehat{\tau}_{it}=Y_{it}-\widehat{Y}_{it}(0), (30)

and, for a target set 𝒮\mathcal{S},

A​T​T^𝒮​(t)=1|𝒮|​∑i∈𝒮τ^i​t.\widehat{ATT}_{\mathcal{S}}(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\widehat{\tau}_{it}. (31)

The graph regularizer addresses counterfactual construction. As in conventional SCM, causal interpretation additionally requires that donor outcomes represent untreated exposure and are not themselves affected by treatment spillovers.

5 GeoEco-SCM: economically adjusted local borrowing

Because GeoEco-SCM uses geography and economic covariates to determine how strongly locations borrow from one another, these inputs must be available independently of the post-treatment outcomes being explained. Otherwise, post-treatment information could inadvertently enter the construction of the counterfactual.

Condition 2 (Graph construction uses only pre-treatment information).

Coordinates, graph topology, and economic covariates used to construct the weighted target graph are observed before treatment or are treatment-invariant attributes. They are available for post-only as well as PRE-observed targets, and neither graph construction nor hyperparameter selection uses post-treatment target outcomes or variables that are consequences of treatment.

Condition 2 is a design requirement rather than a stochastic assumption about the outcome-generating process. Its purpose is to prevent information leakage from the post-treatment period. Because the variables entering the graph are either measured before treatment or treatment invariant, the graph and its edge strengths can be regarded as part of the information set available before the counterfactual is constructed.

5.1 Geographic candidate graph

The geographic graph first determines which locations are allowed to borrow from one another. Let 𝒔i=(xi,yi)⊤\bm{s}_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i})^{\top} be the target coordinate and let di​kg=‖𝒔i−𝒔k‖2d^{g}_{ik}=\|\bm{s}_{i}-\bm{s}_{k}\|_{2}. Each target first selects its kk nearest target locations. An undirected edge is then retained whenever either member of a pair selects the other; the simulations use k=8k=8. This edge set is fixed before economic similarity is considered. GeoEco-SCM therefore does not add new edges between economically similar but geographically non-neighboring locations; economic information only adjusts the strengths of edges that already exist in the geographic graph.

Let EdE_{d} denote the directed neighbor list before symmetrization. In accordance with the implementation, define

hg=median{di​kg:(i,k)∈Ed,di​kg>0}.h_{g}=\operatorname{median}\{d^{g}_{ik}:(i,k)\in E_{d},\ d^{g}_{ik}>0\}. (32)

For Graph-SCM, the raw geographic edge strength is

a~i​kG=exp⁡(−di​kghg).\widetilde{a}^{G}_{ik}=\exp\left(-\frac{d^{g}_{ik}}{h_{g}}\right). (33)

5.2 Pre-treatment economic distance

Let 𝒙i∈ℝp\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} collect pp economic covariates determined before treatment. Here we use continuous quantitative covariates with positive sample variances; in the Monte Carlo study these are proxies for pre-treatment employment density, commercial share, and income. We first standardize each covariate,

𝒛i=diag⁡(σ^1,…,σ^p)−1​(𝒙i−𝝁^),\bm{z}_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat{\sigma}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{\sigma}_{p})^{-1}(\bm{x}_{i}-\widehat{\bm{\mu}}), (34)

where 𝝁^\widehat{\bm{\mu}} and σ^1,…,σ^p\widehat{\sigma}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{\sigma}_{p} are calculated across the target locations. All targets, including post-only targets, have these PRE attributes. Let 𝑺\bm{S} be the sample covariance matrix of the standardized vectors 𝒛i\bm{z}_{i}.

Because highly correlated covariates can make 𝑺−1\bm{S}^{-1} numerically unstable, we slightly shrink the off-diagonal covariances toward zero:

𝑺~=(1−η)​𝑺+η​diag⁡(𝑺)+δcov​𝑰p.\widetilde{\bm{S}}=(1-\eta)\bm{S}+\eta\operatorname{diag}(\bm{S})+\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}\bm{I}_{p}. (35)

Here 𝑰p\bm{I}_{p} is the p×pp\times p identity matrix, 0≤η≤10\leq\eta\leq 1 controls the amount of covariance shrinkage, and δcov>0\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}>0 ensures invertibility. In this study, we set η=0.15\eta=0.15 and δcov=10−6\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}=10^{-6}. This covariance adjustment is distinct from the weight ridge ε\varepsilon in Eq. (20). We then measure economic dissimilarity by

di​ke={(𝒛i−𝒛k)⊤​𝑺~−1​(𝒛i−𝒛k)}1/2.d^{e}_{ik}=\left\{(\bm{z}_{i}-\bm{z}_{k})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{S}}^{-1}(\bm{z}_{i}-\bm{z}_{k})\right\}^{1/2}. (36)

This is a covariance-adjusted distance: differences along highly variable or strongly correlated economic dimensions are not counted as if all covariates were independent and equally scaled. Define

he=median{di​ke:(i,k)∈Ed,di​ke>0}.h_{e}=\operatorname{median}\{d^{e}_{ik}:(i,k)\in E_{d},\ d^{e}_{ik}>0\}. (37)

5.3 Reweighting the existing geographic edges

For β≥0\beta\geq 0, GeoEco-SCM assigns

a~i​k​(β)=exp⁡(−di​kghg−β​di​kehe),(i,k)∈E.\widetilde{a}_{ik}(\beta)=\exp\left(-\frac{d^{g}_{ik}}{h_{g}}-\beta\frac{d^{e}_{ik}}{h_{e}}\right),\qquad(i,k)\in E. (38)

Opposite directed edges are collapsed by averaging their raw strengths. After symmetrization, edge weights are normalized to mean one:

ai​k​(β)=a~i​k​(β)|E|−1​∑(r,q)∈Ea~r​q​(β).a_{ik}(\beta)=\frac{\widetilde{a}_{ik}(\beta)}{|E|^{-1}\sum_{(r,q)\in E}\widetilde{a}_{rq}(\beta)}. (39)

Let 𝑨⁡(β)=[ai​k​(β)]\bm{A}(\beta)=[a_{ik}(\beta)] denote the resulting weighted adjacency matrix. GeoEco-SCM substitutes this graph into the common objective in Eq. (20), with ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} as in Graph-SCM. When β=0\beta=0, Eq. (38) gives the geography-only graph, so the two estimators coincide for the same λ\lambda. Increasing β\beta attenuates economically dissimilar connections more strongly while retaining the geographic edge set. PRE validation selects λ\lambda and β\beta, including the option β=0\beta=0.

6 Hyperparameter selection and computation

6.1 Tuning without post-treatment information

Neither λ\lambda nor β\beta is tuned with post-treatment target outcomes. We keep ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} fixed and use two validation exercises, both constructed entirely from the pre-treatment period. For Graph-SCM, β\beta is fixed at zero, so only λ\lambda is selected.

First, a temporal holdout asks whether the fitted donor weights predict years that were temporarily withheld from otherwise observed pre-treatment histories. Specifically, we remove late pre-treatment years ℋ⊂𝒯0\mathcal{H}\subset\mathcal{T}_{0} and evaluate their prediction. Let 𝑾^−ℋ​(λ,β)\widehat{\bm{W}}^{-\mathcal{H}}(\lambda,\beta) be fitted without the held-out cells. The temporal score is

Rtime​(λ,β)=[1MH​∑(i,t)∈𝒱H(Yi​t−𝒘^i(−ℋ)⊤​𝒀tC)2]1/2,R_{\mathrm{time}}(\lambda,\beta)=\left[\frac{1}{M_{H}}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{V}_{H}}\left(Y_{it}-\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i}^{(-\mathcal{H})\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}, (40)

where 𝒱H\mathcal{V}_{H} is the set of observed held-out cells and MH=|𝒱H|M_{H}=|\mathcal{V}_{H}| is their number. The choice of the holdout window is application dependent and is fixed before tuning; the concrete Monte Carlo setting is reported in the Online Appendix.

Second, we mimic the post-only problem inside the pre-treatment sample. For a small, spatially interspersed subset of complete-history targets, we temporarily hide their entire pre-treatment history, refit the model, and ask how well the hidden values are recovered. We refer to this exercise as pseudo-post-only validation. If 𝒱f\mathcal{V}_{f} is the set masked in fold ff, we refit after setting all Yi​tY_{it} for i∈𝒱fi\in\mathcal{V}_{f} and t∈𝒯0t\in\mathcal{T}_{0} to missing. The fold score is

RPO,f​(λ,β)=[1|𝒱f|​|𝒯0|​∑i∈𝒱f∑t∈𝒯0(Yi​t−𝒘^i,−f⊤​𝒀tC)2]1/2.R_{\mathrm{PO},f}(\lambda,\beta)=\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{f}||\mathcal{T}_{0}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{f}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{0}}\left(Y_{it}-\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i,-f}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}. (41)

The pseudo-post-only targets are selected so that their number of immediate pre-treatment-observed graph neighbors resembles that of actual post-only targets. This matches the local availability of PRE information. It does not ensure that the masked targets represent the economic attributes or selective historical coverage of the actual post-only group; Section 9.6 describes observable checks for applications.

Let R¯PO\overline{R}_{\mathrm{PO}} be the mean of the fold-specific scores RPO,fR_{\mathrm{PO},f}. Both validation scores measure outcome-prediction RMSE on the same scale; neither measures error in the donor weights. The selection score is

S⁡(λ,β)=12​Rtime​(λ,β)+12​R¯PO​(λ,β).S(\lambda,\beta)=\frac{1}{2}R_{\mathrm{time}}(\lambda,\beta)+\frac{1}{2}\overline{R}_{\mathrm{PO}}(\lambda,\beta). (42)

We use the unstandardized average in Eq. (42), assigning equal weight to an absolute RMSE reduction of the same size in either validation task. This is a prespecified default. The search and practical tie-breaking rule are described below; the fold-confirmation details are given in the Online Appendix, Section 4.

6.2 Search strategy

The search compares weak to strong graph regularization and, for GeoEco-SCM, weak to strong economic attenuation. Appropriate numerical ranges depend on the application, so our implementation starts from a scale-adaptive grid and expands a boundary when the best confirmed candidate lies at its edge. The screening, expansion, and fold-confirmation rules are fixed before the search; their numerical settings are given in the Online Appendix, Section 4. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the eligible candidates retained after these steps.

Very similar validation errors provide little reason to impose stronger economic attenuation on the geographic graph. We therefore prefer the smaller β\beta when predictive performance is practically tied. In this study, candidates within 0.5% of the lowest confirmed score are treated as tied. Define

Smin\displaystyle S_{\min} =min(λ,β)∈𝒞⁡S⁡(λ,β),\displaystyle=\min_{(\lambda,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}}S(\lambda,\beta), (43)
𝒞tol\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{tol}} ={(λ,β)∈𝒞:S⁡(λ,β)≤(1+δCV)​Smin},\displaystyle=\{(\lambda,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}:S(\lambda,\beta)\leq(1+\delta_{\mathrm{CV}})S_{\min}\},

where δCV=0.005\delta_{\mathrm{CV}}=0.005 is the prespecified practical tolerance. We select the smallest β\beta in 𝒞tol\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{tol}}; among candidates with that β\beta, we select the lowest score, using the smaller λ\lambda only to resolve any remaining tie. Thus a geography-only specification can be retained when its validation error is sufficiently close to the best score.

In the Monte Carlo implementation, the λ=0\lambda=0 fit is a diagnostic reference. When post-only targets are present, final selection is restricted to λ>0\lambda>0, so their representations use graph-based borrowing. Uniform is therefore a separate comparator rather than an automatically selectable no-borrowing fallback.

6.3 Final numerical optimization

For fixed (λ,β)(\lambda,\beta), Eq. (20) is a convex quadratic program (QP): the objective is quadratic in the unknown weights and the constraints are linear, so any optimum is a global optimum. This form is convenient for reliable numerical solution. Let ri​tr_{it} be a residual variable for each observed target–PRE cell, representing the difference between the observed target outcome and its donor-weighted reconstruction. The problem can be written as

min𝑾,𝒓\displaystyle\min_{\bm{W},\bm{r}}\quad 1N+​∑i∈ℐ+1|𝒪i|​∑t∈𝒪iri​t2+λA+​tr⁡(𝑾⊤​𝑳β​𝑾)+ε​1N​‖𝑾‖F2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{+}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{+}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}}r_{it}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{A_{+}}\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\beta}\bm{W})+\varepsilon\frac{1}{N}\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}, (44)
s.t. ri​t=Yi​t−𝒘i⊤​𝒀tC,(i,t):t∈𝒪i,\displaystyle r_{it}=Y_{it}-\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C},\qquad(i,t):t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}, (45)
𝟏⊤𝒘i=1,𝒘i≥0,i=1,…,N,\displaystyle\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{w}_{i}=1,\qquad\bm{w}_{i}\geq 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,N, (46)

where 𝑳β\bm{L}_{\beta} and A+A_{+} are computed from the selected graph 𝑨⁡(β)\bm{A}(\beta), and the numerical ridge is the same ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} introduced in Section 4.3. Thus Eq. (44) is a residual-variable form of the full objective, including the ridge, for both estimators; Graph-SCM uses β=0\beta=0. The positive coefficient gives a unique mathematical weight solution. The exact conditional interpolation formula is given in the Online Appendix, Section 1.3. At λ=0\lambda=0, a post-only target has no fitting observations or graph penalty, and the ridge selects equal donor weights.

Candidate configurations are screened with a projected Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA; 7) to limit computation during hyperparameter selection. After selecting (λ^,β^)(\widehat{\lambda},\widehat{\beta}), the model is refitted on all available PRE outcomes with OSQP (Operator Splitting Quadratic Program; 22), using tighter convergence tolerances to obtain the reported weights. Algorithmic details, solver tolerances, and the scope of numerical checks are reported in the Online Appendix, Sections 4 and 5.

7 Spatio-temporal and SCM benchmarks

7.1 Ordinary SCM

Ordinary SCM is fitted independently for targets with at least one pre-treatment outcome. It is informative about conditional performance on analyzable targets, but when 𝒪i=∅\mathcal{O}_{i}=\varnothing its own fitting criterion does not determine a target-specific donor representation without an additional cross-unit or outcome-model restriction. It is therefore excluded from the principal full-coverage ranking.

7.2 Uniform donor weights

Uniform weights, wi​j=1/Jw_{ij}=1/J, provide a simple full-coverage reference. This comparator uses no target-specific PRE matching or spatial graph and is particularly informative when true donor weights are unrelated across targets.

7.3 Covariate-balanced synthetic control

Observed attributes offer a direct way to choose donor weights even when a target has no PRE outcomes. We therefore add a covariate-only comparator, denoted Cov-SCM. Each target and donor has two planar coordinate columns, measured in meters, and the same three PRE economic proxies used by the economic-covariate methods. Standardize each of these five columns using its pooled target-and-donor mean and sample standard deviation, dropping any constant column. Let 𝒒i∈ℝpc\bm{q}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p_{c}} be the standardized target attributes and let 𝑸C∈ℝJ×pc\bm{Q}_{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times p_{c}} contain the standardized donor attributes, where pcp_{c} is the number of retained columns. Cov-SCM solves, separately for each target,

𝒘^iCov=arg​min𝒘∈ΔJ⁡{1pc​‖𝒒i−𝑸C⊤​𝒘‖22+εc​‖𝒘‖22},εc=10−10.\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i}^{\mathrm{Cov}}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{w}\in\Delta_{J}}\left\{\frac{1}{p_{c}}\|\bm{q}_{i}-\bm{Q}_{C}^{\top}\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}+\varepsilon_{c}\|\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}\right\},\qquad\varepsilon_{c}=10^{-10}. (47)

Writing 𝒔j\bm{s}_{j} for donor jj’s planar coordinates, coordinate balance compares the target location 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i} with the donor-weighted mean ∑jwi​j​𝒔j\sum_{j}w_{ij}\bm{s}_{j}. Donors may occupy different locations; their weighted mean is balanced jointly with the economic proxies, and balance can be approximate. All standardized attributes receive equal weight, and εc\varepsilon_{c} is fixed rather than tuned using outcomes. This positive numerical ridge makes the weight solution unique and contributes at most 10−1010^{-10} to the objective on the simplex. No target outcome, true donor weight, or true counterfactual enters this fit; the counterfactual prediction uses the resulting weights and donor POST outcomes. The comparison asks whether this direct covariate-balancing rule can replace borrowing donor representations learned from PRE outcomes. Because Cov-SCM uses both geography and economic covariates, it is not an isolated test of the economic edge adjustment. Exact implementation and data-provenance checks are given in the Online Appendix, Section 8.

7.4 Nonseparable spatio-temporal prediction benchmarks

To represent outcome-side spatial prediction, we use a stationary nonseparable spatio-temporal covariance model from the Gneiting class [12]. “Nonseparable” means that spatial dependence is allowed to change with temporal separation rather than being written as a simple product of an independent spatial covariance and an independent temporal covariance. The correlation function is

R⁡(h,u)=exp[−(h/ϕs)as/{1+(u/ϕt)at}γ​as/2]1+(u/ϕt)at,R(h,u)=\frac{\exp\left[-(h/\phi_{s})^{a_{s}}/\{1+(u/\phi_{t})^{a_{t}}\}^{\gamma a_{s}/2}\right]}{1+(u/\phi_{t})^{a_{t}}}, (48)

where hh and uu are spatial and temporal lags, respectively. To keep the benchmark parsimonious and computationally feasible, we fix the spatial and temporal shape parameters at as=at=1a_{s}=a_{t}=1. The parameters ϕs\phi_{s} and ϕt\phi_{t} control the spatial and temporal correlation ranges, γ\gamma controls the degree of spatio-temporal interaction, and the nugget ratio is the variance of independent noise relative to the variance of the correlated spatio-temporal process. These remaining covariance parameters are selected using pre-treatment information only. Their candidate ranges are scaled to the spatial and temporal extent of the data and are expanded when necessary to verify that the selected solution is not driven by a search boundary; the specific Monte Carlo grids are reported in the Online Appendix.

We evaluate two basic strategies, each with and without economic covariates. The first strategy pre-imputes the missing pre-treatment history: missing target outcomes are predicted from the nonseparable spatio-temporal model and ordinary SCM is then fitted to the completed pre-treatment panel. We refer to this as spatio-temporal pre-imputation + SCM; a second version additionally includes PRE economic covariates in the outcome mean model. The spatio-temporal fit uses observed donor and target PRE outcomes, with covariates for both groups in the economic-covariate version. The second strategy bypasses SCM and predicts the untreated post-treatment outcome directly using the target PRE outcomes and donor outcomes available up to the prediction date, again with and without the economic covariates. We refer to these as direct spatio-temporal prediction. In all cases the spatio-temporal model uses the Gneiting covariance function. The direct predictors never use target post-treatment outcomes or future donor outcomes when predicting a given post-treatment date.

The result tables abbreviate spatio-temporal PRE imputation followed by SCM as STI and direct prediction as STD; the suffix -X denotes inclusion of the PRE economic covariates. Both versions of each strategy are reported.

8 Monte Carlo design

To make the simulation concrete without tying it to a particular substantive field, we use a stylized place-based intervention. At the treatment date, a new service or accessibility node is introduced at one location, and the treatment effect declines with distance from that site. A new transit station is one intuitive interpretation, but the same geometry could represent the opening of a health-care facility, a public service center, an environmental remediation site, or another spatially localized intervention. This device is used only to generate transparent spatial heterogeneity in treatment effects and in the observation process; neither Graph-SCM nor GeoEco-SCM relies on transport-specific mechanisms.

8.1 Common spatial and temporal architecture

Each replication contains J=24J=24 untreated donors and N=120N=120 treated targets observed over 1994–2015. All Monte Carlo outcomes are measured on a logarithmic scale. Treatment begins in 2005, giving 11 pre-treatment and 11 post-treatment years. Except in the separated-donor design, donor and target coordinates are sampled independently and uniformly on a 19​km×19​km19\,\mathrm{km}\times 19\,\mathrm{km} interior of a 20​km×20​km20\,\mathrm{km}\times 20\,\mathrm{km} study region. Two pre-existing accessibility centers, which generate baseline spatial structure, are fixed at (4.5,5.5)(4.5,5.5) and (15.5,14)(15.5,14) km, and the newly introduced intervention site is fixed at (10.5,9.5)(10.5,9.5) km. Figure 1 shows one illustrative realization; the two PRE centers and intervention site are fixed across replications.

Different DGPs use separate seed streams, except for the paired supplementary designs D9–D10.

The five primary DGPs described in Section 8.2 each have 100 replications, giving 500 primary datasets. Five supplementary DGPs also have 100 replications each. The complete study therefore contains 10×100=1,00010\times 100=1{,}000 datasets; Cov-SCM uses the same 500 primary datasets. The replication materials record the design-specific seeds and the common replacement seeds for infeasible D9–D10 observation patterns.

8.2 Five primary DGPs

The five primary designs ask when donor relationships can be borrowed across targets, what economic information adds, and when borrowing fails. Table 2 summarizes their roles. The following descriptions introduce the mechanisms before the common equations; the detailed selective-observation and donor-factor formulas are given after their ingredients have been defined.

D1: geographic baseline

True donor weights vary smoothly with geographic market state, and historical coverage is assigned randomly. Nearby observed-history targets should therefore carry information about a post-only target’s donor representation. This is the baseline for sharing PRE-informed representations rather than using uniform weights or balancing observed attributes directly.

D2: informative economic structure

Donor weights depend on both geography and an economic state with substantial variation beyond geography. Nearby targets can therefore require different donor combinations. This design asks whether economic proxies help identify useful local borrowing connections, and compares that use with direct covariate balancing and outcome-side prediction.

D3: selective post-only coverage

The donor-weight and market-state architecture is the same as in D2, but targets near the intervention with low latent PRE signals are more likely to lack histories. The number of post-only targets remains 24. This design examines borrowing from an observed-history group that differs systematically from the post-only population, and the effect of excluding that population from ATT estimation.

D4: complex donor dynamics and nonlinear economic loadings

Donor weights remain constant over time, while donor trajectories use spatially generated coefficients and additional persistent, cyclical, and level-shift factors. Their loadings also contain nonlinear economic structure. This is a joint stress test of outcome structure and temporal dynamics: it asks whether borrowing stable donor representations remains useful when the specified spatio-temporal covariance and linear economic mean are less aligned with the outcome process.

D5: no spatial weight smoothness

Each target receives an independent symmetric Dirichlet weight draw. Neither its neighbors nor observed attributes reveal that particular draw. Uniform weights are the conditional mean of the unknown weights, making this a negative control for unnecessary spatial or economic borrowing.

The Online Appendix completes the coefficient, spatial-function, and factor specifications and gives five supplementary stress tests: geography-only selective coverage (D6), spatially separated donors (D7), abrupt weight boundaries (D8), and a paired local geography–economics experiment (D9–D10). The paired experiment conditions on the feasibility of its post-only selection constraints, as detailed in the Online Appendix. Cov-SCM is evaluated in D1–D5; the original seven full-coverage methods are retained for all ten designs.

8.3 Common outcome model and information available to estimation

Table 3 separates inputs available to the estimators from quantities used to generate and evaluate the simulations. In particular, the observed economic proxies are distinct from the latent states that determine the true donor weights.

The common target-outcome model is

μi​t\displaystyle\mu_{it} =∑j=1Jwi​j⋆Cj​t,𝒘i⋆∈ΔJ,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_{ij}^{\star}C_{jt},\qquad\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}\in\Delta_{J}, (49)
Yi​t​(0)\displaystyle Y_{it}(0) =μi​t+ϵi​t,Yi​t=Yi​t(0)+τi​t,\displaystyle=\mu_{it}+\epsilon_{it},\qquad Y_{it}=Y_{it}(0)+\tau_{it},
ϵi​t\displaystyle\epsilon_{it} ∼iidN⁡(0,0.0082).\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}N(0,0.008^{2}).

Here Cj​t=Yj​tCC_{jt}=Y^{C}_{jt} is donor jj’s log outcome, the true weights are constant over time, and τi​t=0\tau_{it}=0 before treatment. Counterfactual RMSE is evaluated against the latent signal μi​t\mu_{it}.

Donor trajectories combine heterogeneous levels, trends, cycles, and common and donor-specific temporal variation. With calendar year yty_{t} and elapsed time rt=yt−1994r_{t}=y_{t}-1994, the baseline trajectory is

Cj​tbase=αj+bj​rt+qj​rt2+c1​j​sin⁡(rt/2.8)+c2​j​cos⁡(rt/4.2)+ℓj​ftc+uj​t.\begin{split}C_{jt}^{\mathrm{base}}={}&\alpha_{j}+b_{j}r_{t}+q_{j}r_{t}^{2}\\ &+c_{1j}\sin(r_{t}/2.8)+c_{2j}\cos(r_{t}/4.2)+\ell_{j}f_{t}^{c}+u_{jt}.\end{split} (50)

The coefficients αj,bj,qj,c1​j,c2​j\alpha_{j},b_{j},q_{j},c_{1j},c_{2j} determine the donor’s level, linear and quadratic trends, and cycle amplitudes; ℓj\ell_{j} loads on the centered common temporal process ftcf_{t}^{c}. This process combines periodic terms with an AR(1) component of coefficient 0.70 and innovation SD 0.004. The independent donor-specific component uj​tu_{jt} is AR(1) with coefficient 0.55 and innovation SD 0.006.

For D1–D3 and D5, Cj​t=Cj​tbaseC_{jt}=C_{jt}^{\mathrm{base}} and coefficient means depend linearly on the donor market states defined in Section 8.4, with independent Gaussian perturbations. For example, αj=log⁡(220000)+0.18​mj​1−0.10​mj​2+ϵα​j\alpha_{j}=\log(220000)+0.18m_{j1}-0.10m_{j2}+\epsilon_{\alpha j}, where ϵα​j∼N⁡(0,0.102)\epsilon_{\alpha j}\sim N(0,0.10^{2}). D4 changes the baseline coefficient structure and adds temporal factors, as specified below. The Online Appendix gives the remaining coefficient distributions and the complete temporal-process construction. The companion R package supplies the fixed seeds and scripts for reproducing the simulation tables.

8.4 Latent geographic and economic state

Let aa index a generic donor or target location with coordinates 𝒔a=(xa,ya)⊤\bm{s}_{a}=(x_{a},y_{a})^{\top}. In this subsection, standardization pools M=N+J=144M=N+J=144 locations. For a nonconstant vector 𝒗=(v1,…,vM)⊤\bm{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{M})^{\top}, define

z​[𝒗]a\displaystyle z[\bm{v}]_{a} =va−v¯sv,a=1,…,M,\displaystyle=\frac{v_{a}-\bar{v}}{s_{v}},\qquad a=1,\ldots,M,
v¯\displaystyle\bar{v} =1M∑b=1Mvb,sv=[1M−1∑b=1M(vb−v¯)2]1/2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{b=1}^{M}v_{b},\qquad s_{v}=\left[\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{b=1}^{M}(v_{b}-\bar{v})^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

Thus z⁡[⋅]z[\cdot] gives each variable zero sample mean and unit sample standard deviation across the pooled donor and target locations. Each use below applies this operation separately to the variable inside the brackets.

Broad geographic market characteristics are

ga​1\displaystyle g_{a1} =0.70​xa∘+0.20​sin⁡(π​ya∘),\displaystyle=0.70x_{a}^{\circ}+0.20\sin(\pi y_{a}^{\circ}), (51)

where xa∘=(xa−10000)/9500x_{a}^{\circ}=(x_{a}-10000)/9500 and ya∘=(ya−10000)/9500y_{a}^{\circ}=(y_{a}-10000)/9500. To introduce economic variation beyond geography, define

ea​ℓ\displaystyle e_{a\ell} =z⁡[0.20​fℓ​(𝒔a)+0.80​z​[va​ℓ]],\displaystyle=z\!\left[\sqrt{0.20}\,f_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{a})+\sqrt{0.80}\,z[v_{a\ell}]\right], (52)
