with independent va​ℓ∼N⁡(0,1)v_{a\ell}\sim N(0,1). The functions f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} are standardized smooth sinusoidal fields, specified in the Online Appendix. The mixing puts greater weight on location-specific than spatial economic variation. Set κD=0\kappa_{D}=0 in D1 and D5, and κD=0.65\kappa_{D}=0.65 in D2–D4; write 𝒎a=(ma​1,ma​2)⊤\bm{m}_{a}=(m_{a1},m_{a2})^{\top}.

Estimators observe three noisy PRE economic proxies, representing employment density, commercial share, and income:

xa(1)\displaystyle x_{a}^{(1)} =z⁡[0.85​ea​1+νa​1],\displaystyle=z[0.85e_{a1}+\nu_{a1}], (53)
xa(2)\displaystyle x_{a}^{(2)} =z⁡[−0.25​ea​1+0.85​ea​2+νa​2],\displaystyle=z[-0.25e_{a1}+0.85e_{a2}+\nu_{a2}],
xa(3)\displaystyle x_{a}^{(3)} =z⁡[0.55​ea​1−0.35​ea​2+νa​3],\displaystyle=z[0.55e_{a1}-0.35e_{a2}+\nu_{a3}],
νa​p\displaystyle\nu_{ap} ∼iidN(0,0.182),p=1,2,3.\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}N(0,0.18^{2}),\qquad p=1,2,3.

All methods receiving economic covariates use these same observed proxies; the latent states ea​ℓe_{a\ell} and ma​ℓm_{a\ell} are unavailable to estimation.

8.5 True donor weights

For D1–D4, the market states determine a target’s donor representation through

qi​j\displaystyle q_{ij} =−12​[‖𝒎i−𝒎j‖220.602+0.60​(ai−aj0.80)2],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\|\bm{m}_{i}-\bm{m}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{0.60^{2}}+0.60\left(\frac{a_{i}-a_{j}}{0.80}\right)^{2}\right], (54)
wi​j⋆\displaystyle w_{ij}^{\star} =exp⁡(qi​j)∑r=1Jexp⁡(qi​r).\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(q_{ij})}{\sum_{r=1}^{J}\exp(q_{ir})}.

Here aia_{i} and aja_{j} are standardized negative distances to the nearer of the two PRE accessibility centers, using the pooled donor–target sample. Nearby targets tend to have similar market characteristics and donor weights; target–donor physical distance does not enter this score directly. D1 has geography-only market states, whereas D2–D4 also use the economic component in Eq. (52).

D5 instead draws target-specific weights independently:

𝒘i⋆∼indDirichlet⁡(0.2,…,0.2).\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{ind}}}{{\sim}}\operatorname{Dirichlet}(0.2,\ldots,0.2). (55)

This retains the convex donor representation while removing spatial and covariate information about a post-only target’s particular weight draw.

8.6 Treatment effect and observation pattern

Let dinewd_{i}^{\mathrm{new}} be the target’s distance in meters from the intervention site and τi∞\tau_{i}^{\infty} its long-run log treatment effect. Treatment effects decrease with distance and ramp up over five years:

τi∞\displaystyle\tau_{i}^{\infty} =0.015+0.105exp(−dinew/5000),\displaystyle=0.015+0.105\exp(-d_{i}^{\mathrm{new}}/5000), (56)
τi​t\displaystyle\tau_{it} ={0,yt<2005,τi∞​min⁡{1,(yt−2004)/5},yt≥2005.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0,&y_{t}<2005,\\ \tau_{i}^{\infty}\min\{1,(y_{t}-2004)/5\},&y_{t}\geq 2005.\end{cases}

Each replication assigns the 120 targets to 60 complete-PRE, 36 partial-PRE, and 24 post-only locations. Thus 96 targets have at least one PRE observation. Partial histories retain a random 4–8 of the 11 PRE years. Observation groups are randomly assigned in D1, D2, D4, and D5; D3 uses the selective rule below while keeping the same group sizes. The target graph uses k=8k=8 throughout; alternative graph topologies and spatially blocked PRE missingness are not evaluated.

8.7 Selective observation and complex donor trajectories

Selective observation in D3

To implement the selective-coverage mechanism introduced above, define ni=exp(−dinew/3000)n_{i}=\exp(-d_{i}^{\mathrm{new}}/3000), μ¯i,PRE=T0−1​∑t∈𝒯0μi​t\bar{\mu}_{i,\mathrm{PRE}}=T_{0}^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{0}}\mu_{it}, and li=−z⁡[μ¯i,PRE]l_{i}=-z[\bar{\mu}_{i,\mathrm{PRE}}], where standardization here uses the target sample. The selection score is

si=z⁡[ni]+0.90​li+0.50​z​[ni]​li.s_{i}=z[n_{i}]+0.90l_{i}+0.50z[n_{i}]l_{i}. (57)

Exactly 24 targets are sampled without replacement using weights proportional to exp⁡(si)\exp(s_{i}). Keeping this count fixed separates the composition of the post-only population from the amount of missingness. This design examines whether observed-history locations remain informative for a systematically different group and how excluding that group changes the ATT population.

Donor trajectories in D4

The baseline trajectory retains the form in Eq. (50), but coefficient means are generated from smooth spatial bases rather than directly from the economic market state. The actual donor outcome is

Cj​t=Cj​tbase+0.0603​∑h=13ℓj​hLF​Fh​t.C_{jt}=C_{jt}^{\mathrm{base}}+\frac{0.060}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{h=1}^{3}\ell_{jh}^{\mathrm{LF}}F_{ht}. (58)

The three factors Fh​tF_{ht}, standardized over time, have persistent AR(1), cyclical, and level-shift dynamics. Their donor loadings ℓj​hLF\ell_{jh}^{\mathrm{LF}} combine spatial and nonlinear economic structure with donor-specific noise. The nonlinear economic bases are residualized against an intercept and the three observed economic proxies, weakening their direct linear relationship with outcome levels. The target signal still uses the time-invariant weights in Eq. (54). D4 therefore changes both temporal dynamics and the way economic information enters outcomes relative to D2; it does not isolate a temporal-complexity effect. Exact factor and loading formulas are given in the Online Appendix.

8.8 Spatio-temporal benchmark tuning in the Monte Carlo experiments

The numerical covariance grids, mean specification, and likelihood calculation are detailed in the Online Appendix, Section 6. Covariance parameters are fitted to PRE observations within each replication. To check dependence on the candidate range, the spatial correlation-range grid was extended toward shorter distances. This grid development used known simulation truth to assess changes in average POST prediction errors and rankings, and is distinct from PRE-only parameter fitting within each replication. Section 9.5 reports the results of this exploratory sensitivity check.

8.9 Evaluation criteria

For target group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the primary metric is the root mean squared error (RMSE) for prediction of the latent untreated signal,

R​M​S​E𝒢=[1|𝒢|​|𝒯1|​∑i∈𝒢∑t∈𝒯1{Y^i​t​(0)−μi​t}2]1/2.RMSE_{\mathcal{G}}=\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}||\mathcal{T}_{1}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{1}}\{\widehat{Y}_{it}(0)-\mu_{it}\}^{2}\right]^{1/2}. (59)

We evaluate complete-PRE, partial-PRE, post-only, and all-target groups. Tables average replication-specific RMSEs rather than taking a square root after pooling squared errors. Ordinary SCM is evaluated only on its PRE-observed population and is not ranked as an all-target predictor. Every full-coverage comparison uses the same target group within a replication. Post-only performance is the main focus; the all-target average also includes 96 PRE-observed targets and therefore answers a different performance question.

Counterfactual recovery is primary because errors can cancel in aggregate ATT estimates. We also report annual ATT RMSE and signed bias. We report the percentage-scale ATT as

θ𝒢​(t)=100​[exp⁡{|𝒢|−1​∑i∈𝒢τi​t}−1].\theta_{\mathcal{G}}(t)=100\left[\exp\left\{|\mathcal{G}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}}\tau_{it}\right\}-1\right]. (60)

This transforms the mean log effect; it is not the arithmetic mean of site-specific percentage effects. The estimate uses the same transformation of the mean estimated log effect. ATT RMSE is computed over POST years within each replication and then averaged; bias is estimated minus true ATT, in percentage points.

Monte Carlo standard errors quantify variability across the 100 replications. For a paired difference drd_{r} between two methods on dataset rr, let d¯\overline{d} and sds_{d} be the sample mean and standard deviation over the 100 replications. The reported standard error is sd/100s_{d}/\sqrt{100}, and the 95% interval is d¯±t99,.975​sd/100\overline{d}\pm t_{99,.975}s_{d}/\sqrt{100}, where t99,.975t_{99,.975} is the 97.5th percentile of a tt distribution with 99 degrees of freedom. These unadjusted intervals concern mean simulation-performance differences for the specified DGPs and search settings. Only D9–D10 are paired changes to the same underlying ingredients; method comparisons within every DGP are paired by dataset.

9 Monte Carlo results

The five primary designs compare eight full-coverage methods on identical datasets and target groups. Cov-SCM balances coordinates and PRE economic covariates by matching their donor-weighted averages to target attributes; Uniform denotes equal donor weights; STI and STD denote spatio-temporal PRE imputation followed by SCM and direct spatio-temporal prediction, respectively; -X adds PRE economic covariates to the outcome mean model. We focus first on post-only targets, then on ATT recovery and the implications of extending population coverage. Tables report means over 100 replications, with Monte Carlo standard errors or paired intervals as indicated.

9.1 Post-only counterfactual recovery

Table 4 reports counterfactual signal RMSE for the 24 post-only targets in each replication. STI has the lowest mean in the geographic baseline D1, STI-X in D2 and D3, GeoEco-SCM in D4, and Uniform in D5. Economic reweighting improves on Graph-SCM in D2, D3, and D4; the paired intervals exclude zero in these three designs (Table 5). In D1 and D5, GeoEco-SCM instead has slightly higher signal RMSE than Graph-SCM, and both paired intervals exclude zero. Economic adjustment can therefore be detrimental when the proxies do not reveal relevant differences in donor relationships.

The comparison with outcome-side prediction is also conditional on the DGP. STI-X and STD-X have smaller mean post-only errors than GeoEco-SCM in D2 and D3. In D4, GeoEco-SCM has mean RMSE 0.0601, compared with 0.0675 for STI-X; the paired difference is −0.00744-0.00744, with a 95% MC interval of [−0.00960,−0.00528][-0.00960,-0.00528]. This result favors borrowing stable donor representations in D4’s combined setting of spatial donor coefficients, nonlinear economic loadings, and complex temporal factors. Because these features change together, the comparison does not attribute the gain to temporal complexity alone; the linear economic mean used by STI-X is also less aligned with this construction. This advantage concerns counterfactual signal recovery; the corresponding ATT-RMSE difference from STI-X remains uncertain.

Economic edge adjustment improves graph borrowing in D2–D4, but no method dominates across the five designs.

9.2 Can direct covariate balancing replace graph-based borrowing?

The Cov-SCM comparison separates direct balancing of observed attributes from borrowing representations informed by other targets' PRE histories. Graph-SCM and GeoEco-SCM have lower post-only RMSE than Cov-SCM in D1, D4, and D5, with paired intervals excluding zero. Their improvement shows that this covariate-balancing rule does not recover all the useful information available through PRE-informed donor representations. In D2, Cov-SCM improves on geography-only Graph-SCM and has slightly lower mean RMSE than GeoEco-SCM (0.0977 versus 0.1040), but their paired difference remains uncertain: Cov-minus-GeoEco is −0.00631-0.00631, with interval [−0.01265,0.00002][-0.01265,0.00002].

D3 provides the important opposite result. Cov-SCM has mean post-only RMSE 0.0926, compared with 0.1385 for GeoEco-SCM and 0.1810 for Graph-SCM. The Cov-minus-GeoEco interval is [−0.05632,−0.03537][-0.05632,-0.03537]. Selective historical coverage favors post-only targets with low latent PRE signal near the intervention, making their representations harder to borrow from the remaining observed-history targets. Direct use of their own observed covariates may then be more informative. STI-X remains more accurate still, with mean RMSE 0.0750. Its improvement over STI's 0.1699 may reflect using economic information directly in outcome-level prediction, whereas GeoEco-SCM uses it to adjust existing geographic edges.

Uniform has the lowest mean post-only RMSE in D5: 0.0978, compared with 0.1040 for Graph-SCM, 0.1073 for GeoEco-SCM, and 0.2034 for Cov-SCM. D5 draws independent symmetric Dirichlet weights, whose conditional mean is uniform; unrelated neighbors or attributes do not reveal an individual target's draw. Thus outperforming Cov-SCM in this negative control is not evidence that spatial borrowing itself is useful there.

The usefulness of direct covariate balancing depends on the design: it outperforms graph borrowing in D3 and is less accurate in D1, D4, and D5.

9.3 ATT recovery and selective historical coverage

Table 7 reports post-only ATT RMSE and signed bias. RMSE is calculated over POST years within each replication and then averaged. Pointwise counterfactual error and aggregate ATT error need not rank methods identically because errors can cancel across targets. In D2, Cov-SCM has slightly lower counterfactual RMSE than GeoEco-SCM, but its ATT RMSE is higher: 2.998 versus 2.092 percentage points. The paired Cov-minus-GeoEco ATT-RMSE interval is [0.364,1.448][0.364,1.448] (Table 6).

D3 is a failure case for graph-based inclusion. Its post-only group's average true percentage ATT is about +4.87%+4.87\%. GeoEco-SCM's signed bias is −8.164-8.164 percentage points, implying an average estimate of about −3.30%-3.30\% and reversing the sign. Graph-SCM's bias is −11.838-11.838 points. Cov-SCM has bias +0.306+0.306 and ATT RMSE 2.961, compared with GeoEco-SCM's 8.199. STI-X has lower ATT RMSE still, at 2.145 points. Matching the number of PRE-observed graph neighbors during validation does not ensure that pseudo-post-only targets resemble the selectively unobserved group in outcome levels or donor relationships.

In practice, comparing the observed PRE covariate distributions and local anchor availability of post-only and observed-history targets helps assess whether borrowing between the groups is plausible.

Population coverage remains a separate issue. In D3, the true mean percentage ATT over POST years is 3.63% for all targets, 3.32% for the PRE-observed group, and 4.87% for post-only targets. Ordinary SCM estimates about 3.32% for its PRE-observed population. Its proximity to that population's truth does not establish recovery of the all-target effect. The Online Appendix reports the full population comparison, all-target ATT recovery, and group-specific uncertainty summaries.

Including post-only targets extends population coverage, while counterfactual errors in that group can still distort the all-target ATT.

9.4 Overall coverage and economic adjustment

All-target counterfactual RMSE is lower for both graph estimators than Cov-SCM in each primary design. This average includes 60 complete-PRE and 36 partial-PRE targets, where the graph estimators can use own PRE outcomes and Cov-SCM deliberately does not. It therefore complements, rather than replaces, the post-only comparisons. The all-target and separate complete- and partial-PRE results are reported in the Online Appendix. Ordinary SCM remains competitive on PRE-observed targets in those comparisons; extending population coverage is a separate benefit from improving their individual predictions.

The selected economic adjustment also responds to the available structure. GeoEco-SCM selects β=0\beta=0 in 87/100 D1 replications and 64/100 D5 replications, often selecting the geography-only specification when economic similarity supplies no relevant donor information. Selection frequencies for all designs are given in the Online Appendix. One objective therefore covers all three history regimes, and economic reweighting can be switched off by PRE validation; the D1 and D5 results also show that this selection does not eliminate every cost of unnecessary adjustment.

Secondary diagnostics in the Online Appendix, Section 8.6, compare the fitted donor weights with the generating weights. Economic adjustment reduces weight error relative to Graph-SCM in D2–D4, but GeoEco-SCM does not consistently have lower weight error than Uniform, emphasizing that recovery of the generating weights and counterfactual prediction are distinct evaluation targets.

9.5 Numerical checks and supplementary designs

Final weight optimization completed for all 1,000 datasets, with OSQP status solved. Three cases triggered an upper-β\beta search flag during adaptive screening; the flags and final confirmed choices are reported in the Online Appendix.

In the earlier 20-replication-per-design range-sensitivity check, adding shorter spatial correlation ranges changed mean all-target and post-only RMSE by less than 1% for STI, STI-X, STD, and STD-X. The 100-replication study uses the resulting expanded grid. The exploratory grid development using known simulation truth is described in Section 8.8.

The supplementary designs examine selective geography-only coverage, separated donor support, abrupt boundaries, and local economic alignment. Full results and construction details are retained in the Online Appendix.

The local pair favors economic reweighting under both alignment settings. Its point estimate suggests a larger gain under misalignment, but the paired interval still includes zero.

9.6 Practical recommendations

The simulations suggest choosing a method according to whether useful information lies primarily in transferable donor relationships or in predictable outcome levels.

Graph-SCM and GeoEco-SCM are attractive when the donor pool provides plausible counterfactual building blocks and nearby locations with PRE histories can inform a post-only target's donor representation. D4 suggests considering GeoEco-SCM when stable donor combinations coexist with nonlinear economic outcome structure and complex temporal dynamics. Its lower post-only signal RMSE than STI-X concerns this combination of features, rather than an isolated advantage under temporal complexity. Within the graph family, economic reweighting is useful when geography alone misses relevant differences in donor relationships, as in D2–D4. Geography-only Graph-SCM is preferable when economic proxies add no useful donor information, as the D1 and D5 comparisons illustrate.

Geographically separated donors are particularly relevant when nearby potential donors are excluded to limit spillover exposure. D7 illustrates this use: GeoEco-SCM has post-only RMSE comparable to STI-X while using the separated donor pool. The local information comes from PRE-observed targets within the treated region; donor validity remains a requirement, and the graph does not itself model spillover effects.

When geographic and economic characteristics are informative about outcome levels, spatio-temporal prediction should be a leading candidate. STI performs well in D1, and the strong STI-X results in D2 and D3 favor considering economic covariates directly in the outcome mean model. Under selective historical coverage, direct covariate balancing also deserves consideration: D3 shows that a post-only target’s own attributes can be more informative than donor relationships borrowed from an unrepresentative observed-history group.

Before relying on post-only predictions, compare the actual post-only targets with the pseudo-post-only validation targets in terms of their observed PRE economic attributes, distance to the nearest observed-history target, and number of immediate observed-history neighbors. These checks assess whether the validation exercise covers the population to be predicted. D3 shows why matching neighbor counts alone is insufficient when historical coverage selects targets with different donor relationships. Where observed overlap is poor, assess direct covariate balancing and outcome-side prediction alongside graph borrowing.

When spatial and economic borrowing information is weak, retain uniform donor weights as a separate reference, as illustrated by D5. In applications, Uniform can be evaluated on the same temporal and pseudo-post-only PRE holdouts as the graph candidates; the implemented graph-tuning rule does not select it automatically. These PRE comparisons can guide method choice, while selective coverage driven by unobserved signal differences can remain difficult to detect.

10 Conclusion

Graph-SCM constructs synthetic controls for locations with complete, partial, or absent PRE histories within one convex estimation problem. Locations with observed histories inform donor representations, and a geographic graph determines how these representations are shared with post-only locations. GeoEco-SCM retains the geographic topology while adjusting local borrowing strengths using PRE economic similarity. The common formulation provides a coherent constrained approach to heterogeneous historical coverage.

The five primary experiments identify useful conditions and limits. PRE-informed graph borrowing improves on direct covariate balancing in several settings, but selective post-only coverage can favor covariate balancing instead. Spatio-temporal imputation with economic covariates is strong in the economic and selective designs, while borrowing representations is more accurate for the post-only signal in the design combining nonlinear economic loadings with complex donor dynamics. Economic reweighting improves on geography-only borrowing when it carries relevant donor information and can hurt otherwise. Extending coverage is therefore valuable when the borrowed representations are appropriate; it does not itself ensure accurate counterfactuals or treatment effects.

Future research could combine graph-regularized donor representations with explicit models of spatial treatment spillovers. Such an extension would address settings where nearby donor locations are also affected by the intervention. Other extensions include adding economic-neighbor edges, fitting local subgraphs, and examining sensitivity to target density and PRE-history length; the present experiments fix N=120N=120 and 11 PRE periods.

1 Proofs and numerical qualifications for the main-paper propositions

This section proves the two main-paper propositions: conditional graph interpolation and the equivalent graph penalty after substituting the post-only weights. Both describe the case of positive graph regularization and zero numerical ridge. Section 1.3 gives the corresponding conditional interpolation with the numerical ridge used in computation.

Throughout the Online Appendix, vectors and matrices are written in bold italic type, while scalar quantities are written in ordinary math italic. Let G=(V,E,𝑨)G=(V,E,\bm{A}) be the undirected weighted graph defined in the main paper, with weighted adjacency matrix 𝑨=(ai​k)\bm{A}=(a_{ik}), weighted degree matrix 𝑫\bm{D}, and graph Laplacian 𝑳=𝑫−𝑨\bm{L}=\bm{D}-\bm{A}. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote anchor targets with observed PRE outcomes and 𝒰\mathcal{U} post-only targets. The graph-support condition requires every connected component containing a post-only target to contain at least one anchor. After ordering anchors first and post-only targets second,

𝑳=(𝑳𝒜​𝒜𝑳𝒜​𝒰𝑳𝒰​𝒜𝑳𝒰​𝒰),𝑾=(𝑾𝒜𝑾𝒰).\bm{L}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}&\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\\ \bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}&\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\bm{W}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}\\ \bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}\end{pmatrix}. (1)

The unnormalized graph penalty is

Q⁡(𝑾)=∑(i,k)∈Eai​k​‖𝒘i−𝒘k‖22=tr⁡(𝑾⊤​𝑳​𝑾).Q(\bm{W})=\sum_{(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}\|\bm{w}_{i}-\bm{w}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{L}\bm{W}). (2)

For fixed anchors and zero numerical ridge, dividing the graph penalty by its positive total edge weight does not change its minimizer. With positive ridge, the relative scaling is accounted for by ρ\rho in Section 1.3.

1.1 Proof of Proposition 1: donor-weight interpolation

Proof of Proposition 1.

Fix simplex-valued 𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. The fitting loss contains no post-only outcomes, so for λ>0\lambda>0 and ε=0\varepsilon=0 minimizing the full objective over its post-only rows is equivalent to minimizing QQ. Expanding the quadratic form gives

Q⁡(𝑾)=\displaystyle Q(\bm{W})={} tr⁡(𝑾𝒜⊤​𝑳𝒜​𝒜​𝑾𝒜)+2​tr⁡(𝑾𝒜⊤​𝑳𝒜​𝒰​𝑾𝒰)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}})+2\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}})
+tr⁡(𝑾𝒰⊤​𝑳𝒰​𝒰​𝑾𝒰).\displaystyle+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}). (3)

Differentiating with respect to 𝑾𝒰\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}} yields

∂Q∂𝑾𝒰=2​𝑳𝒰​𝒰​𝑾𝒰+2​𝑳𝒰​𝒜​𝑾𝒜.\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}}=2\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}+2\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. (4)

We first show that 𝑳𝒰​𝒰\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}} is invertible under the graph-support condition. For any nonzero vector 𝒙∈ℝ|𝒰|\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{U}|}, extend it to all vertices by setting 𝒛𝒜=𝟎\bm{z}_{\mathcal{A}}=\bm{0} and 𝒛𝒰=𝒙\bm{z}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{x}. Then

𝒙⊤​𝑳𝒰​𝒰​𝒙=𝒛⊤​𝑳​𝒛=∑(i,k)∈Eai​k​(zi−zk)2≥0.\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\bm{x}=\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{L}\bm{z}=\sum_{(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}(z_{i}-z_{k})^{2}\geq 0. (5)

If this quantity were zero, 𝒛\bm{z} would be constant on every connected component. Every connected component containing a post-only target also contains an anchor, and every anchor has zi=0z_{i}=0 by construction. Hence 𝒛\bm{z} must be zero on every component containing post-only targets, implying 𝒙=𝟎\bm{x}=\bm{0}, a contradiction. Therefore 𝑳𝒰​𝒰\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}} is positive definite and invertible.

Setting the derivative equal to zero gives the unique minimizer

𝑾𝒰=−𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜​𝑾𝒜=𝑯​𝑾𝒜.\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}=\bm{H}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. (6)

It remains to show that the rows of 𝑯\bm{H} are convex-combination weights. We first show nonnegativity without introducing additional matrix terminology. Consider one column of 𝑯\bm{H}, corresponding to an anchor aa. Give that anchor boundary value one, all other anchors boundary value zero, and let the post-only values be the corresponding column of 𝑯\bm{H}. The first-order condition says that every post-only value equals the edge-weighted average of its neighboring values. Suppose, for contradiction, that some post-only value were negative, and choose a post-only location attaining the minimum value. All of its neighboring post-only values are at least as large, and all anchor boundary values are nonnegative. A weighted average of those neighboring values therefore cannot equal a strictly smaller negative minimum unless every connected neighbor has exactly the same negative value. Repeating this argument along the connected component would force the same negative value to reach an anchor, contradicting the nonnegative anchor boundary values. The graph-support condition ensures that such an anchor is reached. Hence every entry of 𝑯\bm{H} is nonnegative.

Finally, 𝑳​𝟏=𝟎\bm{L}\bm{1}=\bm{0}. Taking the rows corresponding to 𝒰\mathcal{U} gives

𝑳𝒰​𝒰​𝟏|𝒰|+𝑳𝒰​𝒜​𝟏|𝒜|=𝟎.\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{U}|}+\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{A}|}=\bm{0}. (7)

Multiplying by −𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1} yields

𝑯​𝟏|𝒜|=𝟏|𝒰|.\bm{H}\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{A}|}=\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{U}|}. (8)

Thus each row of 𝑯\bm{H} is nonnegative and sums to one. If each anchor donor-weight vector lies in the simplex ΔJ\Delta_{J}, every row of 𝑾𝒰=𝑯​𝑾𝒜\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{H}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}} is a convex combination of simplex vectors and therefore also belongs to ΔJ\Delta_{J}. ∎

The same first-order condition can be read locally. For a post-only target ii,

𝒘i=1di∑k:(i,k)∈Eai​k𝒘k,\bm{w}_{i}=\frac{1}{d_{i}}\sum_{k:(i,k)\in E}a_{ik}\bm{w}_{k}, (9)

where di=∑kai​kd_{i}=\sum_{k}a_{ik}. Thus the formal result is exactly the weighted-neighbor interpretation given below Proposition 1 in the main paper.

1.2 Proof of Proposition 2: equivalent graph penalty after interpolation

Proof of Proposition 2.

Using the block expansion of Q⁡(𝑾)Q(\bm{W}) from Section 1.1, substitute the minimizing post-only weights

𝑾𝒰=−𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜​𝑾𝒜.\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}=-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}. (10)

Because 𝑳\bm{L} is symmetric, 𝑳𝒜​𝒰=𝑳𝒰​𝒜⊤\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}=\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}^{\top} and 𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1} is symmetric. Straightforward substitution and collection of the cross and quadratic terms yield

min𝑾𝒰⁡Q⁡(𝑾)=tr⁡[𝑾𝒜⊤​(𝑳𝒜​𝒜−𝑳𝒜​𝒰​𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜)​𝑾𝒜].\min_{\bm{W}_{\mathcal{U}}}Q(\bm{W})=\operatorname{tr}\!\left[\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\top}\left(\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}\right)\bm{W}_{\mathcal{A}}\right]. (11)

Defining

𝑳eff=𝑳𝒜​𝒜−𝑳𝒜​𝒰​𝑳𝒰​𝒰−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}}-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{U}}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}} (12)

produces the expression in Proposition 2. ∎

The matrix 𝑳eff\bm{L}_{\mathrm{eff}} is the Schur complement obtained after eliminating the post-only rows. In network theory the same reduction is often called Kron reduction. The terminology is secondary here: substantively, post-only locations affect the indirect pathways linking anchors but do not add PRE outcome observations.

1.3 Numerical ridge and conditional interpolation

Purpose and scale of the numerical ridge.

Short histories, redundant donor trajectories, or weakly determined graph relationships can leave multiple or nearly equivalent donor-weight matrices. The full objective defined in the main text contains ε​R​(𝑾)\varepsilon R(\bm{W}), where R⁡(𝑾)=‖𝑾‖F2/NR(\bm{W})=\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}/N. In this study, we fix ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} for both Graph-SCM and GeoEco-SCM throughout tuning and final estimation. This quadratic term has Hessian (2​ε/N)​𝑰N​J(2\varepsilon/N)\bm{I}_{NJ} in the vectorized weights. It therefore makes the weight objective strictly convex, yielding a unique mathematical minimizer on the feasible set, while retaining a quadratic objective and the same linear constraints.

Let 𝒖=𝟏J/J\bm{u}=\bm{1}_{J}/J denote uniform donor weights. Because each row belongs to ΔJ\Delta_{J},

‖𝒘i‖22=‖𝒘i−𝒖‖22+1J.\|\bm{w}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\bm{w}_{i}-\bm{u}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{J}.

Thus minimizing the ridge penalty is equivalent to favoring weights closer to uniform allocation. It is an explicit computational selection rule, not evidence that uniform weights or the selected weights are closer to the true donor representation. For finite ε>0\varepsilon>0, the penalty can change the fitting and graph terms rather than merely choose between exactly tied solutions.

The simplex constraint gives

1J≤R⁡(𝑾)≤1,εJ≤ε​R​(𝑾)≤ε.\frac{1}{J}\leq R(\bm{W})\leq 1,\qquad\frac{\varepsilon}{J}\leq\varepsilon R(\bm{W})\leq\varepsilon.

Hence ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} contributes at most 10−1010^{-10} to the normalized objective for any feasible weights. More precisely, let F⁡(𝑾)F(\bm{W}) denote the objective without the numerical ridge, let 𝑾0\bm{W}_{0} minimize FF, and let 𝑾ε\bm{W}_{\varepsilon} minimize F+ε​RF+\varepsilon R, all for the same fixed graph and tuning parameters. Comparing their objective values gives

0≤F⁡(𝑾ε)−F⁡(𝑾0)\displaystyle 0\leq F(\bm{W}_{\varepsilon})-F(\bm{W}_{0}) ≤ε⁡{R⁡(𝑾0)−R⁡(𝑾ε)}\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon\{R(\bm{W}_{0})-R(\bm{W}_{\varepsilon})\}
≤ε⁡(1−1/J).\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon(1-1/J).

This justifies the choice as a positive numerical penalty with a bounded effect on the optimized original objective. It is an exact-optimization statement, not a bound on solver error or on differences in weights and POST predictions. Weakly determined directions can still produce appreciable prediction changes.

Conditional post-only interpolation.

For λ>0\lambda>0, define

ρ=ε​A+λ​N,𝑲=−(𝑳𝒰​𝒰+ρ​𝑰|𝒰|)−1​𝑳𝒰​𝒜.\rho=\frac{\varepsilon A_{+}}{\lambda N},\qquad\bm{K}=-(\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}+\rho\bm{I}_{|\mathcal{U}|})^{-1}\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}. (13)

For fixed simplex-valued anchor weights, the exact conditional minimizer is

𝑾^𝒰=𝑲​𝑾^𝒜+(𝟏|𝒰|−𝑲​𝟏|𝒜|)​𝒖⊤.\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{U}}=\bm{K}\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{A}}+(\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{U}|}-\bm{K}\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{A}|})\bm{u}^{\top}. (14)

To derive the formula, center all rows at 𝒖\bm{u}. The centered row-sum constraints are zero, and the conditional quadratic objective has first-order equation

(𝑳𝒰​𝒰+ρ​𝑰|𝒰|)​(𝑾^𝒰−𝟏|𝒰|​𝒖⊤)=−𝑳𝒰​𝒜​(𝑾^𝒜−𝟏|𝒜|​𝒖⊤).(\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U}}+\rho\bm{I}_{|\mathcal{U}|})(\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{U}}-\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{U}|}\bm{u}^{\top})=-\bm{L}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{A}}(\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{A}}-\bm{1}_{|\mathcal{A}|}\bm{u}^{\top}). (15)

The solution is feasible for the simplex. Interpret ρ\rho as an edge from each post-only vertex to an additional fixed boundary with donor weights 𝒖\bm{u}. The maximum-principle proof of Proposition 1 gives 𝑲≥0\bm{K}\geq 0 and 𝑲​𝟏≤𝟏\bm{K}\bm{1}\leq\bm{1}. Equation (14) is therefore a convex mixture of anchor weights and the uniform vector, and is also the constrained conditional minimizer.

At a POST date, write 𝒀^𝒜​t​(0)=𝑾^𝒜​𝒀tC\widehat{\bm{Y}}_{\mathcal{A}t}(0)=\widehat{\bm{W}}_{\mathcal{A}}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C} and Y¯tC=𝒖⊤​𝒀tC\overline{Y}_{t}^{C}=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C}. Multiplying Eq. (14) by 𝒀tC\bm{Y}_{t}^{C} yields

𝒀^𝒰​t​(0)=𝑲​𝒀^𝒜​t​(0)+(𝟏−𝑲​𝟏)​Y¯tC.\widehat{\bm{Y}}_{\mathcal{U}t}(0)=\bm{K}\widehat{\bm{Y}}_{\mathcal{A}t}(0)+(\bm{1}-\bm{K}\bm{1})\overline{Y}_{t}^{C}.

The second term is the contribution from the equally weighted average of donor outcomes. In a general graph, 𝑲\bm{K} also changes the relative contributions of different anchors. Thus this expression need not be a mixture of the unchanged no-ridge harmonic prediction and the donor mean. Moreover, it is conditional on the fitted anchor weights; those weights can themselves change when ridge is added to the full problem.

For a simple illustration with only one post-only vertex ii, let di=∑a∈𝒜ai​ad_{i}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}a_{ia} and 𝒎i=di−1​∑a∈𝒜ai​a​𝒘^a\bm{m}_{i}=d_{i}^{-1}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}a_{ia}\widehat{\bm{w}}_{a}. Then

𝒘^i=didi+ρ​𝒎i+ρdi+ρ​𝒖.\widehat{\bm{w}}_{i}=\frac{d_{i}}{d_{i}+\rho}\bm{m}_{i}+\frac{\rho}{d_{i}+\rho}\bm{u}.

The graph penalty pulls toward the neighbor-weighted vector 𝒎i\bm{m}_{i}, and the numerical ridge pulls toward uniform donor weights. Prediction uses the same two mixing coefficients for 𝒎i⊤​𝒀tC\bm{m}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C} and Y¯tC\overline{Y}_{t}^{C}.

The influence of ridge depends on ρ\rho and the strength of connections to anchors, not solely on ε\varepsilon. The ridge supplies no PRE observations and is not an identification assumption.

At λ=0\lambda=0, each post-only row is determined by the ridge alone and is uniform. Without the ridge, every simplex vector is a minimizer for that row. A component containing only post-only locations similarly has no anchor boundary information: graph smoothing alone cannot determine its common donor vector, even though the ridge selects the uniform solution. Connectivity remains a graph-support diagnostic.

2 Relation to post-only and missing-data methods

Post-intervention-only identification.

Liu et al. (2024) develop a proximal synthetic-control method with post-intervention surrogates. Under bridge and proxy conditions, treatment effects can in some cases be identified using exclusively post-intervention information. Their source of identification is post-treatment surrogate moments. Graph-SCM instead never uses the post-only target’s own POST outcome to learn its weights; its representation is propagated from PRE-observed targets through the graph.

Missing PRE outcomes within SCM.

Liu et al. (2026) study SCM with missing pre-treatment outcomes and the bias and sample-selection consequences of missingness. Robust SCM uses singular-value thresholding to denoise and complete incomplete panels (Amjad et al., 2018). These approaches are natural for partial histories. A completely post-only target removes the unit-specific SCM fit criterion and therefore requires either an additional outcome model, a proxy restriction, or a cross-unit restriction such as the graph assumption used here.

Matrix completion and latent factors.

Nuclear-norm matrix completion (Athey et al., 2021), general missing-pattern latent-factor methods (Xiong and Pelger, 2023), and causal matrix completion under non-random missingness (Agarwal et al., 2023) impose structure on the outcome matrix or latent factors. Vu et al. (2022) add spatial structure to matrix completion for spatially misaligned air-pollution measurements. Graph-SCM instead preserves the donor representation and regularizes the weight field. Spatial vertical regression also shares information across treated locations through donor-coefficient fields (Grossi et al., 2026). The methods therefore encode different extrapolation restrictions.

3 Exact graph construction and economic metric

The public implementation uses a symmetrized geographic kk-nearest-neighbor graph with k=8k=8. Let 𝒔i=(xi,yi)⊤\bm{s}_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i})^{\top} be the coordinate vector of target ii, and let EdE_{d} denote the directed kNN edges. For each directed edge,

di​kg=‖𝒔i−𝒔k‖2,d^{g}_{ik}=\|\bm{s}_{i}-\bm{s}_{k}\|_{2}, (16)

and hgh_{g} is the median positive value of di​kgd^{g}_{ik} over the directed neighbor list EdE_{d}. Symmetrization retains a pair whenever either endpoint selects the other; EE is the resulting set of undirected pairs. After computing raw weights, duplicate opposite-direction edges are collapsed by averaging them.

For the economic metric, let 𝒙i∈ℝp\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} collect the continuous quantitative PRE economic covariates for target ii, each with positive sample variance in this study; here p=3p=3. Each component is centered and scaled using the target sample, producing the standardized vector 𝒛i\bm{z}_{i}. Let 𝑺\bm{S} be the p×pp\times p sample covariance matrix of these standardized covariate vectors, and let 𝑰p\bm{I}_{p} be the p×pp\times p identity matrix. The operator diag⁡(𝑺)\operatorname{diag}(\bm{S}) retains the diagonal entries and sets the off-diagonal entries to zero.

𝑺~=(1−η)​𝑺+η​diag⁡(𝑺)+δcov​𝑰p.\widetilde{\bm{S}}=(1-\eta)\bm{S}+\eta\operatorname{diag}(\bm{S})+\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}\bm{I}_{p}. (17)

For this study, we set η=0.15\eta=0.15 and δcov=10−6\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}=10^{-6}. The covariance adjustment δcov\delta_{\mathrm{cov}} is distinct from the donor-weight ridge ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10} in the full estimation objective. The economic distance between targets ii and kk is the Mahalanobis distance

di​ke=(𝒛i−𝒛k)⊤​𝑺~−1​(𝒛i−𝒛k).d^{e}_{ik}=\sqrt{(\bm{z}_{i}-\bm{z}_{k})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{S}}^{-1}(\bm{z}_{i}-\bm{z}_{k})}. (18)

Let heh_{e} be the median positive economic distance di​ked^{e}_{ik} over EdE_{d}, using the same directed neighbor list as for hgh_{g}. Both bandwidths are determined before economic reweighting. For a fixed nonnegative economic-weighting parameter β\beta,

a~i​k=exp[−di​kg/hg−βdi​ke/he],\widetilde{a}_{ik}=\exp[-d^{g}_{ik}/h_{g}-\beta d^{e}_{ik}/h_{e}], (19)

The final weights are ai​k=a~i​k/{|E|−1​∑(r,q)∈Ea~r​q}a_{ik}=\widetilde{a}_{ik}/\{|E|^{-1}\sum_{(r,q)\in E}\widetilde{a}_{rq}\} for (i,k)∈E(i,k)\in E, with zero entries off EE. Thus the mean edge weight is one and A+=|E|A_{+}=|E|. This normalization keeps the magnitude of the smoothness penalty comparable when β\beta changes.

4 PRE-only tuning algorithm

For N+>0N_{+}>0, the PRE fitting loss is

ℒfit​(𝑾)=1N+​∑i∈𝒜1|𝒪i|​∑t∈𝒪i(Yi​t−𝒘i⊤​𝒀tC)2.\mathcal{L}_{\rm fit}(\bm{W})=\frac{1}{N_{+}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}}(Y_{it}-\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}\bm{Y}_{t}^{C})^{2}.

The graph term is λ​Q​(𝑾)/A+\lambda Q(\bm{W})/A_{+} and the numerical ridge is ε​‖𝑾‖F2/N\varepsilon\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}/N. The observed-history sets and counts in the fitting loss are recomputed within each validation fit after holding out or masking cells. The final replication code follows the sequence below.

  1. 1.

    Construct the geography-only k=8k=8 graph and remove 2002–2004 from the target PRE panel.

  2. 2.

    Fit the λ=0,β=0\lambda=0,\beta=0 reference model, denoting its weights by 𝑾^ref\widehat{\bm{W}}^{\rm ref}, and define the scale λb=max⁡{ℒfit​(𝑾^ref)/2,10−8}\lambda_{b}=\max\{\mathcal{L}_{\rm fit}(\widehat{\bm{W}}^{\rm ref})/2,10^{-8}\}.

  3. 3.

    Screen λ/λb∈{0,0.1,0.3,1,3}\lambda/\lambda_{b}\in\{0,0.1,0.3,1,3\} for β=0\beta=0.

  4. 4.

    Cross every positive screened λ\lambda with β∈{0,0.5,1,2,4}\beta\in\{0,0.5,1,2,4\} and evaluate temporal holdout.

  5. 5.

    For all retained candidates, create spatially interspersed pseudo-post-only folds by masking complete-PRE targets. The selected pseudo targets are chosen so that their immediate PRE-anchor counts resemble those of the actual post-only targets.

  6. 6.

    Compute the combined validation score

    S⁡(λ,β)=0.5​Rtime​(λ,β)+0.5​R¯PO​(λ,β),S(\lambda,\beta)=0.5R_{\rm time}(\lambda,\beta)+0.5\overline{R}_{\rm PO}(\lambda,\beta),

    where RtimeR_{\rm time} is the outcome RMSE on the held-out PRE years and R¯PO\overline{R}_{\rm PO} is the average outcome RMSE across the pseudo-post-only validation folds. Both compare predicted with held-out observed target outcomes on the same log scale; neither is a donor-weight error. When post-only targets are present, only positive-λ\lambda candidates are eligible for final selection; the zero-λ\lambda fit remains a diagnostic reference.

  7. 7.

    Adaptively extend the upper λ\lambda tail by factors of 3 when necessary. The production safety search permits up to 11 tail steps, corresponding to a multiplier as large as 531441. If an economic candidate remains at the upper β\beta boundary, expand by factors of 2, with at most three expansion steps and a maximum β=32\beta=32; reaching a safety limit is recorded.

  8. 8.

    Re-evaluate the leading configurations using three pseudo-post-only folds of eight targets each. Candidates within 0.5% of the best confirmed score are treated as practically tied. Prefer the smallest β\beta, since nearly equal predictive errors offer little support for stronger economic attenuation. Among candidates with that β\beta, choose the lowest score, and then the smaller λ\lambda if a tie remains. This is the practical-tolerance rule defined in the main paper.

  9. 9.

    Refit the selected model on the full available PRE panel using the sparse OSQP quadratic program with tight convergence tolerances.

The equal coefficients in the validation score assign the same value to an absolute RMSE reduction in either task; they do not standardize the variability of the two scores. Applications with a different substantive balance can prespecify ω​Rtime+(1−ω)​R¯PO\omega R_{\rm time}+(1-\omega)\overline{R}_{\rm PO}, with 0≤ω≤10\leq\omega\leq 1. This study uses ω=0.5\omega=0.5; fold confirmation and the preference for smaller β\beta among practically tied candidates are specified above.

Projected FISTA (Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm; Beck and Teboulle, 2009) is used as an accelerated proximal-gradient method for candidate screening. Each iteration takes a gradient step for the smooth quadratic objective, projects each target’s weight vector onto the simplex, and applies the acceleration step. This scheme limits computation when many related fitting problems are solved during hyperparameter selection.

Two pseudo-post-only folds of eight targets are used initially. Screening permits 1500 FISTA iterations at weight-change tolerance 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}; intermediate confirmation permits 3000 at 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}. All simulation candidate fits use cold starts, so candidate comparisons do not use different warm-start histories. After selection, the model is refitted on the full available PRE panel using OSQP (Operator Splitting Quadratic Program; Stellato et al., 2020) with tighter convergence tolerances, as detailed in Section 5. FISTA is used for screening, whereas OSQP determines the reported final weights.

5 Sparse quadratic program for the final fit

Let ℳ={(i,t):t∈𝒪i}\mathcal{M}=\{(i,t):t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}\} be the observed target–PRE cells and let M=|ℳ|M=|\mathcal{M}|. Introduce residual vector 𝒓∈ℝM\bm{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. Vectorize 𝑾\bm{W} rowwise as 𝒘=vecr⁡(𝑾)\bm{w}=\operatorname{vec}_{r}(\bm{W}). If 𝑩\bm{B} is the weighted graph incidence matrix, each row corresponds to an edge e=(i,k)e=(i,k) and is ai​k​(𝒆i−𝒆k)⊤\sqrt{a_{ik}}(\bm{e}_{i}-\bm{e}_{k})^{\top}, where 𝒆i\bm{e}_{i} is the unit vector that selects target ii. Let 𝑰J\bm{I}_{J} be the J×JJ\times J identity matrix. Then

tr⁡(𝑾⊤​𝑳​𝑾)=‖(𝑩⊗𝑰J)​𝒘‖22.\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{L}\bm{W})=\|(\bm{B}\otimes\bm{I}_{J})\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}. (20)

The symbol ⊗\otimes denotes the Kronecker product. Enumerate the observed cells by m=1,…,Mm=1,\ldots,M, and let i⁡(m)i(m) and t⁡(m)t(m) be the target and date of cell mm. The fit residual constraints are sparse because each observed cell involves only the JJ weights of one target:

rm+𝒀t⁡(m)C⊤​𝒘i⁡(m)=Yi⁡(m),t⁡(m).r_{m}+\bm{Y}_{t(m)}^{C\top}\bm{w}_{i(m)}=Y_{i(m),t(m)}. (21)

The Hessian is block sparse and positive semidefinite. The ridge in the objective is ε​‖𝑾‖F2/N\varepsilon\|\bm{W}\|_{F}^{2}/N with ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10}, so its weight-block Hessian contribution is (2​ε/N)​𝑰N​J(2\varepsilon/N)\bm{I}_{NJ} under OSQP's 12​𝒙⊤​𝑷​𝒙\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{P}\bm{x} convention, where 𝒙\bm{x} stacks the weights and residual variables and 𝑷\bm{P} is the quadratic-coefficient matrix. The ridge adds nothing to the residual block. Nonnegativity and row-sum-one constraints are explicit. OSQP uses absolute and relative tolerances 10−810^{-8}. The final QP status in all 1,000 datasets was solved. No λ\lambda search retained a boundary flag. Adaptive β\beta screening retained flags in D4/index 99, D8/index 87 and D10/index 23; the final confirmed β\beta values were 8, 0 and 16, respectively. These screening flags are reported rather than treated as evidence that the search is insensitive to further expansion.

6 Spatio-temporal benchmark details (Gneiting covariance)

Let h≥0h\geq 0 be geographic separation in meters and u≥0u\geq 0 temporal separation in years. The positive parameters ϕs\phi_{s} and ϕt\phi_{t} are spatial and temporal correlation ranges, and 0≤γ≤10\leq\gamma\leq 1 controls their interaction. The correlation model is

R⁡(h,u)=exp[−(h/ϕs)/(1+u/ϕt)γ/2]1+u/ϕt,R(h,u)=\frac{\exp\left[-(h/\phi_{s})/(1+u/\phi_{t})^{\gamma/2}\right]}{1+u/\phi_{t}}, (22)

which is the chosen fixed-shape member of the nonseparable class in Gneiting (2002). Spatial ranges are measured in meters and temporal ranges in years. The reference distance ϕs,0\phi_{s,0} is the median of the positive, finite distances obtained by pooling, over distinct sites in the PRE training panel, the distances from each site to its first five nearest other sites. If fewer than six distinct sites are available, all available other sites are used; a fallback of 2000 m is used if no positive finite reference distance can be obtained. This scale is computed before subsampling PRE cells for covariance tuning. Using PRE data only, a profiled Gaussian marginal likelihood selects covariance parameters from

ϕt\displaystyle\phi_{t} ∈{0.5,1.5,4,8,12,24,48,96,192,384},\displaystyle\in\{0.5,1.5,4,8,12,24,48,96,192,384\}, (23)
ϕs/ϕs,0\displaystyle\phi_{s}/\phi_{s,0} ∈{0.03125,0.0625,0.125,0.25,0.5,1.5,4},\displaystyle\in\{0.03125,0.0625,0.125,0.25,0.5,1.5,4\}, (24)
γ\displaystyle\gamma ∈{0,0.5,1},\displaystyle\in\{0,0.5,1\}, (25)
δnugget\displaystyle\delta_{\rm nugget} ∈{0,0.01,0.15}.\displaystyle\in\{0,0.01,0.15\}. (26)

Here δnugget\delta_{\rm nugget} is the ratio of independent-noise variance to correlated-process variance. For process variance σ2>0\sigma^{2}>0, the correlated covariance is σ2​R​(h,u)\sigma^{2}R(h,u), and σ2​δnugget\sigma^{2}\delta_{\rm nugget} is added to the diagonal of the observation covariance matrix. This yields 10×7×3×3=63010\times 7\times 3\times 3=630 covariance candidates for each version, without or with economic covariates. At most 350 PRE cells are used in covariance tuning. In the economic-covariate version, the same PRE covariates used by GeoEco-SCM enter the mean model for spatio-temporal prediction. The final short-range sensitivity check reduced the minimum spatial-range candidate from 0.125​ϕs,00.125\phi_{s,0} to 0.03125​ϕs,00.03125\phi_{s,0} by adding shorter-range candidates.

The direct spatio-temporal predictor for a post-treatment time tt uses only untreated-control outcomes observed no later than tt plus the target’s observed PRE outcomes. Target POST outcomes and future donor outcomes are prohibited. A programmatic information-set audit checks these restrictions in every replication.

The mean model contains year effects and linear coordinates; the -X versions add the three PRE economic proxies. PRE OLS residuals enter the profiled covariance likelihood. Grid expansion used known simulation truth to examine mean POST errors and rankings; within-replication PRE-only fitting should therefore be distinguished from independent study-level validation. CF and ATT evaluations are taken from the same completed case and matched by design, seed, method, and observation group. The provenance audit has no unmatched results.

7 Exact common Monte Carlo equations and design-specific construction

7.1 Overview of the primary and supplementary DGPs

The ten DGPs are organized into three conceptual families. The first family evaluates when spatial smoothing of donor weights is appropriate or inappropriate: spatially smooth donor weights based on geography only is a positive control, no spatial smoothness in donor weights removes cross-location smoothness in the true donor weights, and abrupt donor-weight change at a spatial boundary introduces a discontinuity that can make smoothing across nearby locations harmful. The second family adds economic or latent structure: donor weights that depend on geography and economics tests whether economic similarity contributes beyond geography, latent temporal factors added makes the outcome process harder to represent by a single global stationary covariance model while preserving stable donor weights, and the paired local geography–economics alignment/misalignment designs change the local correspondence between geography and economics while holding the remaining paired ingredients fixed. The third family changes spatial support or the observation process: the two selective post-only DGPs make the absence of PRE outcomes nonrandom, while donors spatially separated from targets creates a spatial extrapolation problem in which relevant donor support lies away from the target region.

In D4 and D7, baseline donor levels, trends, and temporal loadings are generated from smooth functions of location instead of their direct linear dependence on latent market state in the standard construction. This additional change means that comparisons with D2 do not isolate only added latent factors in D4 or spatial separation in D7. Table S1 states the role of each DGP. The designs organize controlled comparisons of borrowing mechanisms: whether the true weight field is spatially smooth, whether economic similarity contains nongeographic information, whether missingness selects high-effect locations, how donor-outcome structure affects the competing predictors, and whether local graph smoothness breaks at boundaries.

The remaining subsections specify the generating equations and fixed constants. D1–D5 are the primary designs, and D6–D10 are supplementary stress tests. The sequential labels are shared by the paper and public code; the catalog also records legacy labels and the unchanged random seeds.

D9–D10 are constructed to examine local borrowing. Their common observation pattern is selected using the misaligned design, where each post-only location must have nearby PRE-observed neighbors that are both economically similar and dissimilar. Using the aligned design as a reference, donor trajectories are also modified to weaken a linear relationship between target outcome levels and their observed economic covariates. The same modified donor trajectories are used in both designs. The pair preserves coordinates, observation groups, effects, noise, and the collection of economic covariate rows; the assignment of those rows to target locations changes.

The following equations give the full construction behind the main-paper simulation model. The latent untreated signal is

μi​t=∑j=1Jwi​j⋆​Cj​t,Yi​t​(0)=μi​t+ϵi​t,ϵi​t∼N⁡(0,0.0082).\mu_{it}=\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_{ij}^{\star}C_{jt},\qquad Y_{it}(0)=\mu_{it}+\epsilon_{it},\qquad\epsilon_{it}\sim N(0,0.008^{2}). (27)

Only μi​t\mu_{it} has the exact convex donor representation; the realized untreated potential outcome additionally contains noise.

7.2 Why the supplementary designs are included

D6 complements D3 by applying selective historical coverage to geography-only donor weights. D6 can be read alongside the random-coverage geographic baseline D1, just as D3 can be read alongside D2. Together they examine whether a change in the population with observed histories is difficult even when geography is the only source of weight structure. These are separate random-seed designs, not paired interventions on one dataset.

D7 separates donor support from target geography: targets occupy a central disk and donors a surrounding annulus. Donor outcomes can still span the target signal, but prediction at target coordinates requires geographic extrapolation from donor locations. Like D4, this design also changes baseline donor trajectories, so it is a composite stress test rather than an isolated geometry change.

D8 introduces an east/west discontinuity in donor relationships. It checks the cost of treating geographic proximity as evidence for similar weights when nearby targets can belong to different regimes. Economic reweighting may reduce some inappropriate borrowing, but the design does not assume that economic proxies perfectly label the boundary.

D9–D10 form the only paired change of DGP ingredients. The same locations and observation groups are used, and target economic rows are reassigned jointly in D10. This tests sensitivity to local geography–economics alignment without changing the marginal collection of economic characteristics. The shared construction below deliberately retains mixed economic support and weakens a linear outcome-mean channel; it should therefore be read as a controlled local-borrowing experiment.

7.3 Geometry and standardization

Except in D7, donors and targets are drawn uniformly on [500,19500]2[500,19500]^{2} meters. D7 places targets uniformly in the disk of radius 5 km centered at (10,10)(10,10) km and donors in an annulus of radii 7–13 km, truncated to the study square. Two PRE accessibility centers are (4500,5500)(4500,5500) and (15500,14000)(15500,14000) m; the intervention is (10500,9500)(10500,9500) m. Standardized accessibility is negative distance to the nearer PRE center. For a vector 𝒗=(v1,…,vM)⊤\bm{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{M})^{\top}, write z​[𝒗]m=(vm−v¯)/svz[\bm{v}]_{m}=(v_{m}-\bar{v})/s_{v}, where v¯=M−1​∑mvm\bar{v}=M^{-1}\sum_{m}v_{m} and svs_{v} is its sample standard deviation; a constant vector is mapped to zero. Latent market variables and economic proxies are standardized jointly over donors and targets. Donor-only bases use the donor sample, target-selection quantities use the target sample, and time factors use the TT dates. All AR processes below begin with the first innovation rather than a stationary initialization.

7.4 Latent geographic and economic state

Scale coordinates around the center of the region by

xi∘=(xi−10,000)/9500,yi∘=(yi−10,000)/9500.x_{i}^{\circ}=(x_{i}-10{,}000)/9500,\qquad y_{i}^{\circ}=(y_{i}-10{,}000)/9500. (28)

Two smooth geographic market coordinates are

gi​1\displaystyle g_{i1} =0.70​xi∘+0.20​sin⁡(π​yi∘),\displaystyle=0.70x_{i}^{\circ}+0.20\sin(\pi y_{i}^{\circ}), (29)
gi​2\displaystyle g_{i2} =0.65​yi∘+0.18​cos⁡(π​xi∘).\displaystyle=0.65y_{i}^{\circ}+0.18\cos(\pi x_{i}^{\circ}). (30)

At each donor or target location, let q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] control the mixing of the spatial economic component and define two latent economic states

ei​ℓ=z⁡[q​fℓ​(𝒔i)+1−q​z⁡[ui​ℓ]],ℓ∈{1,2},e_{i\ell}=\operatorname{z}\left[\sqrt{q}\,f_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{i})+\sqrt{1-q}\,\operatorname{z}[u_{i\ell}]\right],\qquad\ell\in\{1,2\}, (31)

where the raw ui​ℓu_{i\ell} are independent N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) draws and z⁡[⋅]\operatorname{z}[\cdot] denotes standardization across donors and targets. Both the spatial field and the location-specific Gaussian component are standardized before mixing, as in the simulation code. D1–D8 use q=0.20q=0.20; the local pair D9–D10 uses q=0.60q=0.60 as specified below. The spatial components are

f1​(𝒔i)\displaystyle f_{1}(\bm{s}_{i}) =z⁡[sin⁡(2​π​xi/8500)​cos⁡(2​π​yi/11000)],\displaystyle=\operatorname{z}\left[\sin(2\pi x_{i}/8500)\cos(2\pi y_{i}/11000)\right], (32)
f2​(𝒔i)\displaystyle f_{2}(\bm{s}_{i}) =z⁡[cos⁡(2​π​xi/10500+yi/6000)].\displaystyle=\operatorname{z}\left[\cos(2\pi x_{i}/10500+y_{i}/6000)\right]. (33)

When economic similarity is active, the latent market coordinates are

mi​ℓ=z⁡[gi​ℓ+0.65​ei​ℓ],m_{i\ell}=\operatorname{z}[g_{i\ell}+0.65e_{i\ell}], (34)

and otherwise mi​ℓ=z⁡[gi​ℓ]m_{i\ell}=\operatorname{z}[g_{i\ell}].

Observed pre-treatment economic proxies are noisy functions of the latent state:

xi(1)\displaystyle x^{(1)}_{i} =z⁡[0.85​ei​1+νi​1],\displaystyle=\operatorname{z}[0.85e_{i1}+\nu_{i1}], (35)
xi(2)\displaystyle x^{(2)}_{i} =z⁡[−0.25​ei​1+0.85​ei​2+νi​2],\displaystyle=\operatorname{z}[-0.25e_{i1}+0.85e_{i2}+\nu_{i2}], (36)
xi(3)\displaystyle x^{(3)}_{i} =z⁡[0.55​ei​1−0.35​ei​2+νi​3],\displaystyle=\operatorname{z}[0.55e_{i1}-0.35e_{i2}+\nu_{i3}], (37)

with νi​p∼N⁡(0,0.182)\nu_{ip}\sim N(0,0.18^{2}). The estimators see these proxies but never the latent economic states.

7.5 True donor weights

Let aia_{i} be standardized pre-treatment accessibility, defined as negative distance to the closest pre-existing accessibility center. For the baseline smooth-weight DGPs, the target–donor matching score is

qi​j=−12​[(mj​1−mi​10.60)2+(mj​2−mi​20.60)2+0.60​(aj−ai0.80)2].q_{ij}=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{m_{j1}-m_{i1}}{0.60}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{m_{j2}-m_{i2}}{0.60}\right)^{2}+0.60\left(\frac{a_{j}-a_{i}}{0.80}\right)^{2}\right]. (38)

The true donor weights are the softmax

wi​j⋆=exp⁡(qi​j)∑r=1Jexp⁡(qi​r).w_{ij}^{\star}=\frac{\exp(q_{ij})}{\sum_{r=1}^{J}\exp(q_{ir})}. (39)

Here, target–donor physical distance does not enter Eq. (38). Geography matters because nearby targets tend to have similar latent market states and hence similar donor representations. The construction therefore evaluates smoothness of donor representations, not a nearest-donor rule.

The no-spatial-smoothness negative control instead draws

𝒘i⋆=(wi​1⋆,…,wi​J⋆)⊤∼i​n​dDirichlet⁡(0.2,…,0.2),\bm{w}_{i}^{\star}=(w_{i1}^{\star},\ldots,w_{iJ}^{\star})^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle ind}}{{\sim}}\operatorname{Dirichlet}(0.2,\ldots,0.2), (40)

so that target weights are concentrated but unrelated across nearby locations.

7.6 Treatment effect and observation pattern

Let dinewd_{i}^{\mathrm{new}} be distance in meters from target ii to the newly introduced intervention site. The long-run log treatment effect is

τi∞=0.015+0.105exp(−dinew/5000).\tau_{i}^{\infty}=0.015+0.105\exp(-d_{i}^{\mathrm{new}}/5000). (41)

For calendar year yty_{t}, the treatment path is

τi​t={0,yt<2005,τi∞​min⁡{1,(yt−2004)/5},yt≥2005.\tau_{it}=\begin{cases}0,&y_{t}<2005,\\ \tau_{i}^{\infty}\min\{1,(y_{t}-2004)/5\},&y_{t}\geq 2005.\end{cases} (42)

The observed target outcome is

Yi​t=μi​t+τi​t+ϵi​t,ϵi​t∼N⁡(0,0.0082).Y_{it}=\mu_{it}+\tau_{it}+\epsilon_{it},\qquad\epsilon_{it}\sim N(0,0.008^{2}). (43)

Targets are assigned to 50% complete PRE, 30% partial PRE, and 20% post-only groups. A partial-PRE target retains a random 4–8 of the 11 pre-treatment years. In the random-entry DGPs, group membership is random. In the selective post-only designs, the post-only set has a fixed size but is sampled with higher probability for sites that are both close to the intervention site and have low latent pre-treatment counterfactual levels. This creates a deliberate difference between A​T​TPREATT_{\mathrm{PRE}} and A​T​TALLATT_{\mathrm{ALL}} without changing the number of missing histories.

f~tc\displaystyle\widetilde{f}_{t}^{c} =0.012​sin⁡(rt/3.1)+0.008​cos⁡(rt/5.0)+utc,\displaystyle=0.012\sin(r_{t}/3.1)+0.008\cos(r_{t}/5.0)+u_{t}^{c}, (44)

αj\displaystyle\alpha_{j} =log⁡(220000)+0.18​mj​1−0.10​mj​2+ϵα​j,\displaystyle=\log(220000)+0.18m_{j1}-0.10m_{j2}+\epsilon_{\alpha j}, ϵα​j\displaystyle\epsilon_{\alpha j} ∼N⁡(0,0.102),\displaystyle\sim N(0,0.10^{2}), (47)

7.8 Alternative outcome architecture for added-latent-factor and spatially-separated-donor designs

For D4 and D7, baseline donor-outcome coefficients change from the standard architecture to smooth spatial bases, removing their direct linear dependence on economic market state. Thus D4 and D7 are composite designs; their differences from D2 cannot be attributed solely to added factors or separated geometry.

Define standardized spatial bases

B1​j\displaystyle B_{1j} =z⁡[sin⁡(π​xj/9000)+0.7​cos⁡(π​yj/11000)],\displaystyle=z[\sin(\pi x_{j}/9000)+0.7\cos(\pi y_{j}/11000)], (55)

Each normal-distribution term below denotes an independent draw. Then

αj\displaystyle\alpha_{j} =log⁡(220000)+0.10​B1​j+N⁡(0,0.102),\displaystyle=\log(220000)+0.10B_{1j}+N(0,0.10^{2}), (58)
bj\displaystyle b_{j} =0.004+0.002​B2​j+N⁡(0,0.00452),\displaystyle=0.004+0.002B_{2j}+N(0,0.0045^{2}), (59)
qj\displaystyle q_{j} =−0.00005+N⁡(0,0.000082),\displaystyle=-0.00005+N(0,0.00008^{2}), (60)
c1​j\displaystyle c_{1j} =0.008​B3​j+N⁡(0,0.0122),\displaystyle=0.008B_{3j}+N(0,0.012^{2}), (61)
c2​j\displaystyle c_{2j} =−0.006​B1​j+N⁡(0,0.0102).\displaystyle=-0.006B_{1j}+N(0,0.010^{2}). (62)

The common-factor loading is 1+0.12​z​[sin⁡(π​xj/10000)+0.6​cos⁡(π​yj/12000)]+N⁡(0,0.102)1+0.12z[\sin(\pi x_{j}/10000)+0.6\cos(\pi y_{j}/12000)]+N(0,0.10^{2}).

The latent-factor DGP additionally adds

Cj​tL​F=Cj​tbase+0.0603​∑r=13ℓj​rL​F​Fr​t,C^{LF}_{jt}=C_{jt}^{\mathrm{base}}+\frac{0.060}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{r=1}^{3}\ell_{jr}^{LF}F_{rt}, (63)

For D4, the donor outcome entering the target signal is Cj​t=Cj​tL​FC_{jt}=C^{LF}_{jt}. Each loading combines a weighted spatial basis and a nonlinear economic-archetype basis plus donor-specific noise; their exact coefficients are given below. The economic archetype bases are nonlinear radial-basis or sinusoidal functions of the latent economic state, residualized against the intercept and three observed economic proxies. The temporal factors include persistent AR(1), cyclical, and level-shift dynamics. This construction makes economic proximity informative about donor composition without making the observed economic proxies simple linear regressors for the outcome level.

7.9 Design-specific modifications

7.9.1 Abrupt boundary (D8)

For the spatial-boundary design, donor regime labels are defined by whether

mj​1+0.30​mj​2m_{j1}+0.30m_{j2} (64)

is above or below its donor median. A target is assigned an east/west regime according to whether xi≥10000x_{i}\geq 10000 m. Write RiR_{i} and RjR_{j} for these target and donor regime labels within this construction. The baseline score in Eq. (38) is modified to

qi​jB=qi​j+2.50​I​(Ri=Rj).q_{ij}^{B}=q_{ij}+2.50\,I(R_{i}=R_{j}). (65)

Thus adjacent targets on opposite sides of the x=10x=10 km boundary can have abruptly different donor representations even though their geographic coordinates are close.

7.9.2 Selective post-only sampling (D3 and D6)

Let

ni=exp(−dinew/3000),n_{i}=\exp(-d_{i}^{\rm new}/3000), (66)

standardized across targets as z⁡(ni)z(n_{i}). Let μ¯i,P​R​E=|𝒯0|−1​∑t∈𝒯0μi​t\bar{\mu}_{i,PRE}=|\mathcal{T}_{0}|^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{0}}\mu_{it} be the mean latent untreated PRE signal and define li=−z⁡(μ¯i,P​R​E)l_{i}=-z(\bar{\mu}_{i,PRE}). The selection score is

si=z⁡(ni)+0.90​li+0.50​z​(ni)​li.s_{i}=z(n_{i})+0.90l_{i}+0.50z(n_{i})l_{i}. (67)

Exactly 20% of targets are selected as post-only without replacement using sampling weights proportional to exp⁡(si)\exp(s_{i}). The fixed count isolates composition effects from changes in the amount of missingness.

7.9.3 Paired local construction (D9–D10)

The paired local design increases the spatial share of the latent economic field from q=0.20q=0.20 to q=0.60q=0.60, making the aligned member a genuinely aligned baseline. The complete target economic row

(ei​1,ei​2,xi(1),xi(2),xi(3))(e_{i1},e_{i2},x_{i}^{(1)},x_{i}^{(2)},x_{i}^{(3)}) (68)

is then permuted jointly across target locations for the misaligned member. Joint permutation preserves the complete empirical distribution and all within-row relationships exactly.

The mismatch permutation is selected using only pre-specified DGP diagnostics. For each target, the ten nearest geographic neighbors are identified and their Euclidean distances in the three-dimensional observed economic-proxy space are calculated. Edges below the 35th percentile of all local economic distances are labeled economically similar and those above the 65th percentile dissimilar. A location is mixed-support eligible when it has at least two similar and two dissimilar local neighbors. Candidate deterministic interleavings are scored by

𝒟=Δ​d¯e​c​o​nl​o​c​a​l+0.20​pm​i​x​e​d+0.02​b¯m​i​x​e​d,\mathcal{D}=\Delta\overline{d}_{econ}^{local}+0.20\,p_{mixed}+0.02\,\overline{b}_{mixed}, (69)

To define these quantities, let nisn_{i}^{s} and nidn_{i}^{d} be the counts of similar and dissimilar neighbors among the ten local neighbors. Then pm​i​x​e​d=N−1​∑iI⁡(nis≥2,nid≥2)p_{mixed}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}I(n_{i}^{s}\geq 2,n_{i}^{d}\geq 2) and b¯m​i​x​e​d=N−1​∑imin⁡(nis,nid)\overline{b}_{mixed}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\min(n_{i}^{s},n_{i}^{d}). The first term is the candidate-minus-aligned change in the mean of all local economic distances. The thresholds and counts are recomputed for each candidate. No fitted Graph/GeoEco estimate, RMSE, treatment effect, or counterfactual truth enters this choice.

Both paired members use the same post-only selection set, determined from the mismatch-design feasible candidate set but a common geographic/station-proximity priority. The same complete, partial, and post-only IDs are therefore used in the two members. The paired audit additionally verifies equality of coordinates, retained PRE counts, treatment effects, target noise, donor trajectories, and the multiset of economic covariate rows.

Sampling in D9–D10 is conditional on the existence of a feasible set of 24 post-only targets, each retaining at least two economically similar and two dissimilar geographic neighbors with PRE observations. Any seed with no such set is excluded for both members and replaced by the next common seed, retaining the fixed candidate threshold and neighborhood constraints; the common indices are 1–102 excluding 50 and 70. Those two draws admit at most 23 post-only targets, and indices 101 and 102 replace them. Excluded and replacement seeds are recorded in the replication code.

To reduce direct linear prediction of untreated outcome levels from the observed economic proxies in the paired experiment, donor outcome vectors are partially orthogonalized to the target-level economic direction implied by the aligned pair. The realized increase in PRE R2R^{2} from adding economic proxies to a regression on year effects and coordinates is recorded as a diagnostic; it does not exclude replications. Let 𝑬r​e​s∈ℝN×3\bm{E}_{res}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} contain the residuals from separate regressions of the three aligned-target economic proxies on an intercept and the two coordinates, and let 𝑾r​e​f∈ℝN×J\bm{W}_{ref}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J} be the true aligned-design weight matrix. Define

𝑨E=𝑬r​e​s⊤​𝑾r​e​f.\bm{A}_{E}=\bm{E}_{res}^{\top}\bm{W}_{ref}. (70)

The matrix 𝑨E​𝑨E⊤\bm{A}_{E}\bm{A}_{E}^{\top} is 3×33\times 3. For each donor vector 𝒄t=(C1​t,…,CJ​t)⊤\bm{c}_{t}=(C_{1t},\ldots,C_{Jt})^{\top}, calculate the ridge-stabilized projection

𝒑t=𝑨E⊤​(𝑨E​𝑨E⊤+κ​𝑰3)−1​𝑨E​𝒄t,\bm{p}_{t}=\bm{A}_{E}^{\top}(\bm{A}_{E}\bm{A}_{E}^{\top}+\kappa\bm{I}_{3})^{-1}\bm{A}_{E}\bm{c}_{t}, (71)

and replace

𝒄t←𝒄t−0.75​𝒑t,\bm{c}_{t}\leftarrow\bm{c}_{t}-0.75\bm{p}_{t}, (72)

with κ=10−10​max⁡{tr⁡(𝑨E​𝑨E⊤)/3,1}\kappa=10^{-10}\max\{\operatorname{tr}(\bm{A}_{E}\bm{A}_{E}^{\top})/3,1\} for the three economic proxies. The same transformed donor outcomes are used for both paired members. Here 𝝁\bm{\mu} denotes the matrix of latent untreated target signals and 𝑪\bm{C} the donor-outcome matrix. This truth-side construction preserves the exact SCM identity 𝝁=𝑾⋆​𝑪\bm{\mu}=\bm{W}^{\star}\bm{C} but reduces the possibility that a spatio-temporal mean model with economic covariates performs well simply because the DGP placed the target economic proxies directly in the outcome level.

7.10 Details of the additional latent factors (D4)

For donor coordinates (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}), the three standardized spatial bases are

S1​j\displaystyle S_{1j} =z⁡[sin⁡(2​π​xj/20000)​cos⁡(π​yj/20000)],\displaystyle=z[\sin(2\pi x_{j}/20000)\cos(\pi y_{j}/20000)], (73)
S2​j\displaystyle S_{2j} =z⁡[cos⁡(π​xj/10000+yj/14000)],\displaystyle=z[\cos(\pi x_{j}/10000+y_{j}/14000)], (74)
S3​j\displaystyle S_{3j} =z⁡[sin⁡{π⁡(xj+yj)/18000}].\displaystyle=z[\sin\{\pi(x_{j}+y_{j})/18000\}]. (75)

Let bj(c1,c2)=exp[−{(ej​1−c1)2+(ej​2−c2)2}/(2×0.702)]b_{j}(c_{1},c_{2})=\exp[-\{(e_{j1}-c_{1})^{2}+(e_{j2}-c_{2})^{2}\}/(2\times 0.70^{2})]. The residualization deliberately weakens a linear economic outcome-mean channel while retaining nonlinear economic information. It is part of the positive-control construction and does not establish a general advantage over covariate-rich outcome models.

8 Additional Monte Carlo results

8.1 All-target results and the added covariate baseline

The five primary designs use eight full-coverage methods on the same 100 datasets. Table S2 complements the main-paper post-only comparisons with all-target RMSE. Table S3 reports Cov-SCM separately for each observation group, including its Monte Carlo standard errors and signed ATT bias.

For a target group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the signal RMSE within one replication is

[1|𝒢|​|𝒯1|​∑i∈𝒢∑t∈𝒯1{Y^i​t​(0)−μi​t}2]1/2.\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}||\mathcal{T}_{1}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{1}}\{\widehat{Y}_{it}(0)-\mu_{it}\}^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

Tables average these replication-specific values. An MCSE is the sample standard deviation across replications divided by the square root of the replication count. Paired intervals use d¯±tn−1,.975​sd/n\overline{d}\pm t_{n-1,.975}s_{d}/\sqrt{n}, where dd is the within-dataset method difference, sds_{d} its sample standard deviation, and tn−1,.975t_{n-1,.975} the Student-tt quantile; here n=100n=100.

8.2 Cov-SCM implementation and provenance

The covariate fit uses only the two observed planar coordinate columns in meters and three PRE economic proxy columns. Balance concerns donor-weighted attribute averages, so individual donors need not share the target location. Let 𝒒i∈ℝpc\bm{q}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p_{c}} be a standardized target attribute vector and 𝑸C∈ℝJ×pc\bm{Q}_{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times p_{c}} the donor attribute matrix, after dropping constant columns. Cov-SCM minimizes pc−1​‖𝒒i−𝑸C⊤​𝒘‖22+10−10​‖𝒘‖22p_{c}^{-1}\|\bm{q}_{i}-\bm{Q}_{C}^{\top}\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}+10^{-10}\|\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2} over 𝒘∈ΔJ\bm{w}\in\Delta_{J} independently for each target. Columns are standardized jointly across the 120 targets and 24 donors. The mean squared standardized imbalance has equal feature coefficients and a fixed ridge of 10−1010^{-10}. The simplex-constrained quadratic program is solved by a base-R active-set algorithm with an absolute duality-gap tolerance of 10−1310^{-13}.

Cov-SCM was evaluated on the same 500 primary datasets and target groups as the other methods. The accompanying replication materials document data alignment and implementation checks.

8.3 Paired comparisons with Cov-SCM

These comparisons use the same design, seed, and target group for both methods. Differences are Cov-SCM minus the reference method; negative values favor Cov-SCM. The full paired CSVs include all seven original full-coverage comparators and all four observation groups. The tables below focus on post-only targets.

8.4 Original ten-design counterfactual comparisons

The seven original full-coverage methods were evaluated in all ten designs. Cov-SCM is evaluated only in the five primary designs, so the tables in this subsection retain the seven-method comparison throughout. All cells use 100 replications. Complete- and partial-PRE comparisons include ordinary SCM on the same observed-history group.

8.5 Paired local geography–economics alignment experiment

The final local pair holds geography, membership in the post-only, partial-PRE, and complete-PRE groups, treatment effects, target noise, donor outcomes, and the multiset of economic covariate rows fixed. Only the spatial assignment of the target economic state changes between the two members. As described in Section 7.1, the common observation pattern is selected to retain both economically similar and dissimilar observed neighbors in the misaligned design. Donor trajectories are modified in the same way in both members to weaken a linear economic outcome relationship. These choices provide economically informative observed neighbors for edge reweighting, while weakening the linear outcome-mean channel that can benefit STI-X. Section 7 gives the construction.

Economic misalignment makes prediction harder for both methods. Post-only RMSE rises from 0.0496 to 0.0602 for Graph-SCM and from 0.0454 to 0.0543 for GeoEco-SCM. The paired contrast

Δpair=\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{pair}}={} (R​M​S​EGeoEco−R​M​S​EGraph)misalign\displaystyle\left(RMSE_{\mathrm{GeoEco}}-RMSE_{\mathrm{Graph}}\right)_{\mathrm{misalign}}
−(R​M​S​EGeoEco−R​M​S​EGraph)align\displaystyle-\left(RMSE_{\mathrm{GeoEco}}-RMSE_{\mathrm{Graph}}\right)_{\mathrm{align}} (80)

is −0.00169-0.00169 for post-only targets, with a Monte Carlo interval of [−0.00346,0.00008][-0.00346,0.00008]. Local misalignment degrades both estimators, while GeoEco-SCM remains more accurate in both post-only samples. The point estimate suggests a larger GeoEco advantage under misalignment, but the interval includes zero, so the experiment does not establish an increase in that advantage.

8.6 Donor-weight recovery and concentration

The generating weights 𝒘i⋆\bm{w}_{i}^{\star} are known in these simulations. For a target group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we calculate the mean of the target-specific weight RMSEs within each replication,

E𝒢W=1|𝒢|​∑i∈𝒢[1J​∑j=1J(w^i​j−wi​j⋆)2]1/2.E_{\mathcal{G}}^{W}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}}\left[\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}(\widehat{w}_{ij}-w_{ij}^{\star})^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

This averages target-specific RMSEs, rather than pooling squared weight errors before taking a square root. We also calculate the effective number of donors, Dieff=1/∑j=1Jw^i​j 2D_{i}^{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sum_{j=1}^{J}\widehat{w}_{ij}^{\,2}; its range is 1 to JJ, and Uniform has Dieff=24D_{i}^{\mathrm{eff}}=24. This describes concentration across donors. Because locations and generating weights change across the original replications, their raw between-replication variation is not a fixed-design estimate of sampling variance.

Table S15 reports post-only results from all 1,000 saved datasets for Graph-SCM, GeoEco-SCM and Uniform. It includes paired GeoEco-minus-Graph and GeoEco-minus-Uniform weight-RMSE differences. Ordinary SCM has no post-only weights; its PRE-observed weight diagnostics, together with group-specific summaries for the other methods, are included in the replication materials.

Economic adjustment reduces post-only weight RMSE relative to Graph-SCM in D2–D4, but GeoEco-SCM does not consistently improve recovery of the generating weights relative to Uniform. Correlated donor trajectories can produce similar counterfactual predictions under substantially different weights, so weight-error rankings need not follow the counterfactual-error rankings. These diagnostics therefore provide supplementary information about the fitted representations, while counterfactual prediction remains the primary evaluation target.

9 ATT recovery and observation selection

The percentage ATT transforms each year’s mean log effect before evaluating errors. RMSE is first calculated over POST years within each replication; means and Monte Carlo standard errors are then taken across replications. The first two tables include Cov-SCM for the five primary designs. The remaining tables preserve the original seven-method comparison across all ten designs.
